#1538. Chelsea’s feisty friendly ends in penalty shoot-out confusion

Chelsea’s Far East tour ended in farce and confusion with players waiting around for a penalty shoot-out that never happened.

The chaos came at the end of a hard-earned, bad-tempered draw against Malaysian champions Johor Darul Ta’zim, with an own-goal in the 89th minute sparring the west London side’s blushes.

That goal also was supposed to set up penalties. But after minutes of waiting around – and Kevin Campello, Chelsea’s head of first-team operations, saying “it’s written in the contract” – the players walked off the pitch.

That confusion ended a feisty affair in which tensions threatened to boil over and that, at certain points, paid little attention to the “friendly” aspect of the clash with seven yellow cards shown. At one point the visitors’ new set-piece coach Austin MacPhee exchanged angry words with some of Johor’s coaching staff. The CFC TV commentary team suggested that the spot-kicks were abandoned because of the match’s heated atmosphere.

Austin MacPhee was ready to throw hands😂 pic.twitter.com/CFDgTOwmxE

Having played just 24 hours earlier in Jakarta – a 3-0 win over AC Milan – it was no surprise to see Xabi Alonso name a fresh XI, a mixture of players who may well be offloaded before the end of the transfer window, those needing to prove themselves, and youngsters given much-needed game time.

And considering Johor are one game away from setting a new world record of 109 matches unbeaten in the top flight – a run that would surpass the current mark set by Ivorian side Asec Mimosas in the early 1990s – it was also no shock to see the Malaysian team offer a stern, pre-season test for the west Londoners.

After a good start Chelsea were second best in a first half in which Johor should have been at least two goals to the good. The Malaysian champions controlled the first 45 minutes and were 1-0 up after 14 minutes – a low cross from the left side-footed home by Arif Aiman.

The hosts gave the young, inexperienced Chelsea backline a torrid time, especially on the flanks and Óscar Arribas was guilty of not capitalising on a great chance to double Johor’s lead, his shot after cutting in from the right going wide.

While they looked vulnerable at the back, Chelsea also struggled to keep possession in attack. But they got an equaliser they scarcely deserved after Liam Delap was manhandled to the ground in the box by Kevin Medina. The striker, who may well leave Stamford Bridge before the transfer window slams shut, fired home the spot-kick allowing the visitors to go into the break on level terms.

For the most part, the second half followed a similar pattern to the first – Jofor having the better chances, while tensions on the pitch continued to run high.

It was, however, Chelsea who took the lead after the break, Delap once again scoring from the spot, this time after Jamie Gittens was brought down in the area.

Johor, though, kept on creating, thanks in part to a fairly porous visitors’ backline, and levelled through a deflected Arribas free kick, before going 3-2 up thanks thanks to a well-taken Bérgson strike.

Had it stayed that way Chelsea could have had few complaints. But as the clock approached 90 minutes, the visitors had one last attack. Mykhailo Mudryk, just on as a substitute, delivered a cross from the left that Antonio Glauder could only steer into his own net. That was supposed to set up the penalty shoot-out that did not take place and the chance for one of the sides to claim a hollow victory.

Considering a raft of changes and that fact this was far from the first XI, it is hard to know what to make of this. But among the positive things Alonso could take from the game was the impressive form of Nicolas Jackson and good centre-forward play of Delap. The negative was, however, a poor defensive display.

Chelsea return to Stamford Bridge on Saturday for their last pre-season friendly, against Real Sociedad, before the Premier League season starts away at local rivals Fulham on August 24.

Johor Darul Ta’zim: Syihan Hazmi; Arribas, Israfilov (Carlos Akapo 82), Medina, Antonio Glauder, Silva (La’Vere Corbin-Ong 89); Arif Aiman, Petrovic, Méndez (Nené 78), Marcos Guilherme (Bérgson); Zahedi (Stoichkov 62). Substitutes: Abad, Davies, Hidalgo, Nahuel Leiva, Lowry, Mohamadou Sumareh, Stuart Wilkin.Booked: Israfilov, Antonio Glauder, Silva.Goals: Arif Aiman (14), Arribas (65), Bérgson (86).Chelsea: Sharman-Lowe (Slolina 46); Subuloye, Adarabioyo, Anselmino (Watson 29); Geovany Quenda, Dario Essugo, Nicoll-Jazuli, Gittens (Mudryk 87); Estêvão, Delap, Jacskon (Satpaev 86). Substitutes: Curd, Diakite, Kavuma-McQueen, Sarr, Walsh.Booked: Estêvão, Delap, Jackson, Geovany Quenda, Watson.Goals: Delap (42 pen, 62 pen), Antonio Glauder (89 og).

There will NOT be a penalty shootout. No one is quite sure why.

Anyway, that was an entertaining draw, plenty of good things for Chelsea (the play of Delap and Jackson) as well as worrying signs (open and vulnerable at the back).

The commentators on CFC TV are now not so sure!

That was an entertaining pre-season friendly. There was a bit of niggle and that added to the action.

There will be penalties, apparently, if it stays the same score...

Will there be a late winner? There will be four minutes of added time.

Mudryk just on picks up the ball on the left and, with four Chelsea players in the box, crosses into the danger area. It’s a good ball and asks too many questions of the hosts as Glauder diverts the ball into his own net.

It’s what the host have, on the balance of play, deserved, but it’s a gift from Chelsea. Essugo loses the ball in the final third and Bergson, on as sub pick it put driving at the box before hitting a low shot from outside the area, the ball nestling in the left corner of the net.

Chelsea have been better this half than the first 45, they’ve been able to control the pace of the game well since the break.

The pace has slowed down since the break, Chelsea seeing more of the ball. They work it right before Watson loses possession on the edge of the area.

The referee clearly forgot about the hydration break and the two teams are having a belated one now. Delightful...

I reckon there’s another goal left in this match. It’s been entertaining fare and the hosts have given as good as they’ve got, if not more.

This has been a lively match, better than most run-of-the-mill pre-season friendlies. Chelsea seeing a fair bit of possession at the moment, can they fashion a chance?

Yes they can. But it’s a longish shot from Gittens that is easily saved by Hamzi in the JDT goal.

More niggle in this match that hasn’t really had many tough challenges. After a few handbags the referee takes control and the argy bargy peters out.

It’s the least the hosts deserve. They have a free-kick 25 yards out, Arribas takes it with his right it’s at the wall but in turning away from the ball Delap deflects it into the far-right corner giving Slonina no chance.

Fluky goal but the hosts have deserved their bit of luck.

Delap again with the goal, this time he goes low, but still to the keeper’s right.

Penalty for Chelsea. Gittens cuts back in the box onto his right and is clipped by the defender. Clear-cut penalty.

Half-chance for Delap on the edge of the area. He playes a one-two with Jackson before opening up his body and letting fly, the shot going well wide.

Another good chance for the hosts and it’s not shock to write that it’s come from the industry of Arribas on the right. He fires in a low cross that evades everyone in the box.

Estevao goes down in the box, it looks as though it could well be a penalty but the referee waves play on. The Brazilian is the shown a yellow card for possibly lashing out having not got the decision he wanted.

The hosts have asserted themselves well this half, in much the same way as they did in the first 45 minutes.

Another good chance for the hosts and again it’s all too easy as Zahedi is one-on-one with the keeper. The striker, however, dithers a bit too long and Slonina makes a fine save. JDT have had plenty of chances to add to their sole goal...

Chelsea have had a ragged start to this half.

Good work from JDT who keep the ball well in midfield before a throughball is played to the on-rushing Zahedi but Slonina comes out well.

They’re back under way in Johor, and there’s an early chance for Jackson who gets the ball in the box, but the ball gets stuck underneath him and he cannot get in a good attempt in on goal.

And that is the last action of an entertaining half. Chelsea started well before the hosts opened the scoring. JDT then took control of the half and should, if truth be told, have extended their lead. But Delap did well to earn the penalty that he subsequently scored and should have made it 2-1 with the last kick of the 45.

Worrying signs at the back, however, for Alonso. Will Chelsea go to four at the back after the break?

The answer to that question (see last post) was so very nearly yes...

Jackson plays in a peach of a through ball with the outside of his right foot, Delap is one-on-one with the keeper and looks for all the world as though he has to score. BUT he scuffs his shot wide.

There will be three minutes of added time. Can Chelsea head into the break with an unexpected lead?

Free-kick for Chelsea on the JDT byline. The ball is put deep into the box, it’s headed back by Tosin before the ball is blazed over the bar.

A minute later Tosin then let’s fly form 25 yards, the ball goes well over the bar.

The hosts should have been more than 1-0 to the good and now they’re drawing. Goals change matches...

Having won the penalty Delap fires the spotkick home, sending the keeper the the wrong way.

Penalty to Chelsea and it’s all thanks to good centre-forward play by Delap. He gets the ball in the box and Medina manhands him to the ground. The referee doesn’t hesitate before pointing to the spot.

Chelsea have struggled to create anything since the opening 15 minutes. They have no control at the front and none at the back currently.

As I type that JDT have another good chance to turn the 1-0 lead into a 2-0 lead. Arribas, whose been a menace all game, dances toward the Chelsea box before delaying the pass too long.

JDT are finding a lot of joy on the flanks, there are three at the back for Chelsea and on the outside are two youngsters. The hosts are working the space well.

Yet again Chelsea are made to look decidedly average. A simple ball over the top on the right opens up the visitors’ defence and Arribas is in on goal, he cuts in and lets fly with his left peg, the shot going wide.

That should have been 2-0 to the Malaysian powerhouses.

Worrying signs for Chelsea who have struggled to keep possession up top and looked vulnerable at the back.

Yet more good work from JDT who are being given space by Chelsea. Marcos Guilherme slaloms into the west Londoners’ box and Tosin again doesn’t look the most assured but the JDT player cuts the ball back and the visitors can clear the danger.

Another good attack from the hosts who get in a shot in on goal, it’s deflected and loops into the grateful arms of Sharman-Lowe in the Chelsea goal.

There’s a break in play with Anselmino down and suffering what looks like a hamstring injury. He is eventually replaced by Reggie Watson.

Meanwhile, the home fans are in fine voice and waving several HUGE flags.

Yep, everyone’s least favourite part of the World Cup in the U, S of A is back. To be fair it’s humid in Johor so taking on fluids during the first 45 minutes is no bad idea.

There’s a bit of argy-bargy not really what you should get in a ‘friendly’. There hasn’t been a bad chellenge in the match so far so not sure where that came from...

Yet more good work from the hosts, this time it’s down the right, Arribas getting the better of Anselmino before shooting at the near post - the attempt hitting the side netting.

After a lively start Chelsea have been second best.

Poor defending from the visitors there but the chance was well snapped up by JDT.

Lovely break from the hosts. They break down the left at pace, before the ball is threaded through to the back post and Arif Aiman sidefoots into the back of the net with aplomb.

So very nearly an opener for Chelsea. They break at pace thanks to Estevao who drives down the middle before playing in Jackson. The striker cuts in from the left and shoots, the attempt is saved well by Hamzi and Estevao’s follow up is wide. Is a goal coming?

Free-kick for Chelsea some 35 yards out. Too far fro a shot on goal? Of course it is. The ball is floated into the box and the visitors earn a corner.

What can they create from this set piece? ‘Not much’ is the initial answer as the ball is cleared by JDT but Chelsea win possession back and the ball is fed to Estevao on the left, the Brazilian goes for go with his trusty left peg but the bal goes high and wide.

JDT attack down the left, it’s a lovely ball in that forces a fine header to clear the danger from Adarabioyo.

No sooner had I sent that last post than Chelsea break through the middle. The ball is fed through to Delap who gets a left-footed shot in on goal forcing a good save from the JDT keeper Hamzi.

Quiet, low-key start to the match. No real shock there, it is a pre-season friendly.

JDT give the ball away in their half and Chelsea have a half-decent platform to launch an attack from. They cannot fashion a chance and also lose possession.

They’re under way in southern Malaysia, Chelsea are in their vibrant blue and the hosts are wearing a fetching pink number. There was a late change for the visitors, Mamadou Sarr has been replaced by Olutayo Subuloye.

CHELSEA XI TO FACE JOHOR: Sharman-Lowe; Sarr, Tosin, Anselmino; Quenda, Nicoll-Jazuli, Essugo (c), Gittens; Estevao; Jackson, Delap; subs: Slonina, Curd, Subuloye, Diakite, Watson, Mudryk, Walsh, Kavuma-McQueen, Satpayev

...Luis Garcia. The Spaniard has history with Chelsea, remember the ‘ghost goal’?

Arriving for duty! 🫡 pic.twitter.com/M2XEkLC18n

Your Chelsea side today! 🔵 pic.twitter.com/0OvvGVmgpc

A mixture of players who may well be offloaded before the end of the transfer window, those needing to prove themselves, and youngsters you may not have heard of.

Johor Darul Ta’Zim – more commonly known as JDT – are the Man Utd of Malaysia (at least that’s according to a Malaysian friend of mine). In 2013, they were going nowhere and were the dictionary definition of a stagnant club, low on confidence and trophies. That was until the Crown Prince bought the club and, over the next 13 years, transformed it into the powerhouse it is today.

As if to underline JDT’s dominance over Malaysian football they are one game away from the world record unbeaten run in a top flight. The new season of the Malaysian Super League gets under way later this month and should they avoid defeat in their opening match they will extend their unbeaten run - which began in April 2021 - to 109 games and surpass the world record set by Ivorian side Asec Mimosas in the early 1990s.

Chelsea’s pre-season tour of South East Asia ends today with a match against Johor Darul Ta’zim in Malaysia. The clash comes barely 24 hours after the west Londoners beat AC Milan 3-0 in Jakarta, a much-needed win coming on the back of defeats against Juventus and Tottenham.

A fine volley from Moises Caicedo and a double from João Pedro either side of half-time led Xabi Alonso’s side to victory in the Indonesian capital.

The game was fairly even in the first half and looked set to head into the break level at 0-0 but Pedro’s header from Caicedo’s corner put Chelsea in front.

Alonso’s side then doubled their advantage seconds into the second half as Pedro scored his second, assisted by Pedro Neto.

Just minutes later, Chelsea had their third courtesy of a well-worked corner routine. Romeo Lavia’s delivery was met by Caicedo on the volley, with the Ecuadorian’s finish with the outside of the boot finding the bottom corner.

Today, the west London side face Malaysian powerhouses Johor at the Sultan Ibrahim Stadium, more on them later, but considering the tight turnaround from yesterday’s match today’s clash will provide a stern test.

“The idea, with the game against Milan and then one in Johor, was to arrive at this weekend with players not being ready for 90 minutes until now,” Alonso explained after the win in Jakarta.

“We wanted to have a logical progression in their loads; so we had our plan and we’ve stuck to that.

“We have another idea [against Johor]; that was decided yesterday [Friday]. The idea is that many young players were coming to have chances to play tomorrow. If not, we’d have been short, as playing two games in two days is quite intense. So we will need them.”

Stay here for all the team news and action with kick-off set for 1pm.

#1537. Flexible rubber blades for tidal turbines

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

The global transition towards sustainable energy systems has identified tidal power as a uniquely predictable and substantial renewable energy resource1. However, the highly unsteady sea environment subjects turbines to severe hydrodynamic loads, greatly increasing capital and maintenance costs2,3. Large-scale state-of-the-art turbines at present rely on complex, expensive active pitch systems to mitigate these fluctuations. Here we present a reliable, passive alternative: flexible rubber blades featuring chordwise trailing-edge deformation. We experimentally demonstrate that these flexible blades achieve an equivalent total energy yield over simulated tidal cycles compared with rigid blades with active pitch control, while mitigating high-frequency fatigue-inducing load fluctuations by up to one-third. This passive load regulation arises from aeroelastic deformation that flattens blade camber under load, enabling structural robustness without added mechanical complexity. These findings suggest that chordwise-flexible blades can enhance the durability and performance of tidal turbines, offering a promising pathway towards more reliable and cost-effective tidal energy generation.

The global imperative to transition towards sustainable energy systems has intensified research and development in renewable energy technologies. Among these, tidal energy presents a uniquely predictable and substantial resource. Unlike other renewables such as wind and solar, tidal currents are governed by an astronomical cycle, which offers a consistent and forecastable power source4,5. The scale of this resource is significant. Tidal power is estimated at 50 TW h yr−1 in Europe6 and as much as 220 TW h yr−1 in the USA alone7. Near-term deployment targets are 1 GW by 2035 in the UK3, with international roadmaps project deployments eventually exceeding 300 GW worldwide by 20508. These highlight the potential of tidal energy in contributing to energy security and renewable energy portfolios.

Despite their promise, the harsh hydrodynamic environment presents an important barrier to the economic viability of this renewable energy source. A primary challenge is the hydrodynamic load fluctuations that arise from large variations in flow velocity, turbulence, turbine yaw with respect to the incoming stream, velocity shear along the water depth2, wave-induced oscillating currents9, and wake interaction within turbine arrays10. These fluctuating loads are a primary design consideration and are associated with accelerated fatigue, reduced operational lifespans and unplanned downtime. These reliability concerns result in blade and turbine designs with high capital costs, which directly increase the levelized cost of energy (LCOE)3.

To address the challenge of the dynamic loads, various mitigation strategies have been developed. Active control typically deploys systems to actively regulate the pitch11 or camber12 of the blades, therefore, to regulate power output, control mean loads and improve start-up performance. Although the active control systems are effective in certain operational envelopes, the reliability of sophisticated sensors and actuators in the harsh undersea environment remains a concern. Furthermore, the response times of the activator limit effectiveness against rapid, high-frequency load fluctuations13,14.

To address these concerns, there has been an increased focus on developing passive control mechanisms. Passive control is mainly realized in two ways: introducing changes in the blade pitch or modifying the blade camber. Passive pitch control involves designing blades that can rotate around their spanwise axis in response to changing hydrodynamic loads, thereby altering their angle of attack. This is typically achieved by incorporating a pre-loaded torsional spring mechanism at the blade root. Theoretical work in refs. 15,16 are among the first to introduce the concept. Both demonstrated that complete cancellation of the load fluctuation is possible without compromising the mean power. This is followed by a numerical study in ref. 17, which confirmed more than 80% load fluctuations can be reduced in sheared flow conditions, with additional benefits such as faster wake recovery, which improves turbine array performance. Reference 18 has contributed a general framework for the design of passive pitching systems, identifying the locations of the pivot point for maximizing load mitigation. Experimental validations in ref. 19 have confirmed the ability of passive pitching systems in the reduction of time-averaged loadings.

Passive pitching systems are effective for low-frequency, large-scale adjustments and power regulation by adjusting the global angle of attack of the blades. However, the added inertia due to the displacement of the pitching axis required by effective pitching systems, as well as the bearing friction, limits the response of the system to high-frequency disturbances, such as turbulent eddies or rapid shear variations. Moreover, despite being simpler than active control systems, passive pitch blades still introduce extra moving parts and potential failure points in harsh undersea environments. Research has identified that for wind turbine applications, most of the failures originate from the pitch system20, highlighting the significant operational advantage of a robust, passive design.

An alternative design philosophy can be found in nature, where organisms from fish to trees passively reconfigure their shape through distributed material compliance to manage fluid dynamic forces21,22. Drawing from these biological principles, passive morphing flexible blades offer an alternative strategy, where flexibility is distributed along the blade, allowing each blade section to adapt automatically through fluid–structure interaction. Therefore, a faster response time can be achieved with a fixed-pitch blade that does not require hinges and bearings. Passive morphing blades are common in wind energy applications23,24, in which the blade twists to feather in response to a wind gust. This technique, known as aeroelastic tailoring, requires ad hoc structural design, whose scalability and reliability for large tidal turbines is yet to be demonstrated. In fact, for similar power-rated turbines, the bending moment experienced by tidal turbines is higher than that of wind turbines. Therefore, the need for a scalable, reliable, passive system that can mitigate both rapid, localized turbulent fluctuations and slower, large-scale changes in inflow velocity on large-scale tidal turbines remains unmet.

This study directly addresses this challenge by proposing a blade with chordwise flexibility, rather than spanwise flexibility, as in aeroelastic tailoring. The frontal and thickest part of the blade, which provides structural integrity, is rigid. Instead, the trailing edge is flexible from root to tip. Specifically, we provide the first comprehensive experimental demonstration that a carefully designed chordwise-flexible blade can achieve both control of the mean power and thrust with the quasi-steady variations of flow velocities over the tidal cycle (for example, the diurnal tidal cycle) and mitigation of the high-frequency (turbulence) hydrodynamic load fluctuations on tidal turbines, while enabling the same yield as a conventional rigid blade equipped with active pitch control. To demonstrate this potential, we experimentally evaluated the performance of these chordwise-flexible blades against a rigid baseline in the FloWave Ocean Energy Research Facility at the University of Edinburgh. The turbine was tested across a range of nominal inflow velocities u∞ = 0.5–1.0 m s−1, and tip-speed ratios (λ) from 3 to 9, with the flexible blades designed for optimal performance at u∞ ≈ 0.85 m s−1. Our analysis first addresses the low-frequency load mitigation over a tidal cycle before examining the high-frequency load fluctuations and the underlying physical mechanisms of the deformation of the blade. Overall, we demonstrated a new pathway to enhance turbine reliability and survivability, reducing capital costs associated with the active pitch system, and reducing maintenance costs by removing hinges, bearings and actuators, ultimately reducing the LCOE.

The structural design of a tidal turbine is primarily dictated by low-frequency loads, which, in this context, refers to the quasi-steady hydrodynamic loads that change as the mean inflow velocity varies over a tidal cycle. To investigate the potential for load control in this regime, the time-averaged performance of the flexible blades was compared against a rigid baseline. Figure 1 shows the time-averaged power (CP), thrust (CT), and root bending moment (CM) coefficients as a function of tip-speed ratio λ, at all tested inflow velocities. The results demonstrate that the introduction of blade flexibility does not compromise the primary function of energy capture of the turbine. As shown in Fig. 1a, at the rated velocity (uR = 0.878 m s−1) and above, the power coefficient of the flexible blade closely matches that of the rigid blade, achieving a comparable peak CP of approximately 0.37. Notably, the limited value of the maximum CP of both the rigid and flexible blades compared with full-scale state-of-the-art turbines is due to the low Reynolds number at which the model-scale turbines were tested (Methods).

The key advantage of the flexible blade design is its ability to passively regulate peak loadings. At the rated velocity, the thrust coefficient of the flexible blade is comparable to that of the rigid blade near the optimal power-producing tip-speed ratio (λ ≈ 5.5−6), as shown in Fig. 1b. However, the performance of the flexible blades diverges from rigid ones for λ values beyond this optimal range. This high λ region is typically explored by the turbine control strategy to cap power when inflow velocity exceeds the rated velocity. Under these conditions, the flexible blade thrust passively decreases, whereas the rigid one increases. This demonstrates a load-shedding mechanism that can protect the turbine structure during the most demanding high-flow conditions and will be discussed in detail in the next section, in which we simulate the power and thrust a tidal turbine experiences over a tidal cycle. However, at off-design conditions, the flexible blade exhibits higher CT and CM values than at its design speed. While this results in higher thrust coefficients at lower velocities, the absolute forces, which scale with velocity squared (\(F\propto {u}_{\infty }^{2}\)), are much smaller during lower flow periods and are not as important for the structural design of the turbine as the peak loads experienced at or above rated velocity. Therefore, the ability of the flexible blade technology to match power performance while simultaneously offering a passive mechanism to reduce the most important structural loads represents a marked advancement for designing more durable and cost-effective tidal turbines.

a–c, Time-averaged coefficients of power (a), thrust (b) and root bending moment (c) as a function of the tip-speed ratio for rigid and flexible blades at different flow speeds.

To quantify the practical benefits of the passive load mitigation of the chordwise-flexible blade in realistic inflow, we simulate the performance over a representative tidal cycle and compare it against a rigid blade turbine with the same control strategy and a state-of-the-art, actively pitch-controlled turbine (see Supplementary Note 2 for modelling of the active pitch-and-speed control turbine). The sinusoidal inflow velocity represents the flow seen by a tidal turbine during a tidal cycle is shown in Fig. 2a, which is

a–d, Time history over a simulated tidal period of the freestream speed (a), the quasi-steady power (b), the tip-speed ratio (c) and the quasi-steady thrust (d). Data are presented for a rigid-blade turbine with only an active speed controller, a state-of-the-art active pitch-and-speed controller, and rubber blades with an active speed controller. All data are divided by the corresponding rated value.

The cut-in velocity of the turbine is selected at u∞/uR = 0.2. The turbine operates at λ = 5.5 when the velocity is lower than rated. At the rated speed, all turbine configurations are operated at the same tip-speed ratio (λR) and provide the same quasi-steady power (PR) and thrust (TR). At higher than rated velocities, λ is such that P/PR = 1. The maximum velocity is set at u∞/uR = 1.2, representative of typical tidal turbine operating conditions.

The simulation first confirms that the passive design of the flexible blade does not compromise its primary function of energy capture. The normalized power profiles shown in Fig. 2b coincide for the rubber blade with speed control and the state-of-the-art active pitch control turbine, where the turbine speed is shown in Fig. 2c. As the total energy harvested is proportional to the integral of the power curves over the tidal cycle, the overlap of the curves confirms a negligible difference in overall energy yield. This demonstrates that the load-mitigation benefits of flexible blades can be achieved without a penalty to energy capture in a real-world setting.

The advantage of the flexible blade design is revealed by the differences in the quasi-steady thrust (Fig. 2d) between the turbine configurations. The state-of-the-art active pitch system limits structural loads by actively feathering the blades into the flow while maintaining the rated rotational speed. For a rigid blade, using only an overspeed-control strategy, the fixed geometry cannot adapt to the increasing flow; solely increasing the tip-speed ratio results in an increasing thrust that peaks at approximately 1.65 times the rated value (Fig. 2c). By contrast, with a comparable speed-control strategy, the passive system of the flexible blade achieves the same quasi-steady power and similar quasi-steady thrust as the active control.

It is also important to note that flexible blades show a slightly higher thrust coefficient at lower, off-design velocities (Fig. 1b) than the baseline rigid blade. However, the absolute thrust force, which scales with velocity squared, is smaller during these periods than the peak values over the tidal cycle. As the maximum loading dictates the primary structural design requirements of a turbine, the nearly identical peak thrust of the passive flexible blade to that of the complex, state-of-the-art active pitch system suggests comparable outcomes for turbine longevity and maintenance costs, representing a marked advancement towards more durable and cost-effective tidal energy systems. Overall, these results indicate that the chordwise-flexible blades can offer a compelling and robust alternative to the state-of-the-art active pitch-and-speed control turbine system.

An effective passive system must also address high-frequency load fluctuations, which are a primary driver of fatigue damage. In this context, high frequency refers to the unsteady load components that occur at frequencies of the order of the period of revolution, such as those induced by turbulence, velocity shear or wake interaction, and so on. Figure 3 quantifies the effectiveness of the flexible blades by presenting the standard deviation of load fluctuations relative to the reference rigid blades at rated velocity. To reflect realistic conditions over a tidal cycle, the data for u∞/uR ≤ 1 are presented at the optimal tip-speed ratio (λ = 5.5) for maximum power extraction, whereas the data for conditions above the rated velocity (u∞/uR = 1.06) are presented at the higher tip-speed ratio (λ = 8) that is used to cap power. Figure 3 shows a substantial reduction of unsteady loads for all three components when the turbine is operating under its most demanding conditions. At the rated velocity (u∞/uR = 1.0), where the turbine operates at its optimal λ for maximum power extraction, the flexible blades provide effective fluctuation reduction across power, thrust and root bending moment (mitigated by approximately 18%, 23% and 28%, respectively). Furthermore, even when the inflow velocity increases beyond the rated velocity (u∞/uR = 1.06), the load fluctuation mitigation remains substantial. This demonstrates the powerful and robust damping ability of the flexible blades during both the maximum-power and power-capping phases of operation, when the absolute magnitude of fluctuating forces is greatest. At the lowest velocities (for example, u∞/uR = 0.51), where the blade operates in a stalled condition, fluctuations are known to increase relative to the rigid blade. However, their absolute magnitude is small, reaching only about 15–35% of the fluctuation level of the rigid blade at its rated velocity. A more detailed analysis, presented in Supplementary Note 3, confirms that this mitigation is robust across a wide range of tip-speed ratios under these high-flow conditions.

a–c, Standard deviation of power (a), thrust (b) and root-bending moment (c) of flexible and rigid blades, for the optimum tip-speed ratio (λ = 5.5). All quantities are divided by those of the rigid blade at rated velocity.

To illustrate the physics of the passive load regulation mechanism demonstrated previously, the deformation of the flexible blade is visualized at the tip section. Figure 4 shows the phase-averaged digital image correlation (DIC) measurements of the tip of the same flexible blade at a constant azimuthal angle, in which the blade is horizontal with downward velocity. The successful application of this technique using fully submerged cameras represents a significant experimental achievement, as most underwater DIC studies to date have been performed through observation windows rather than submerging the camera in the fluid25. In this way, complex optical distortions and refractive index mismatches associated with viewing ports are avoided, thereby achieving a more accurate measurement. In this study, the DIC system measured the deformation of the suction side of the blade. The full blade profile was then reconstructed by adding the known thickness distribution of the undeformed blade to the measured deformed chord line.

Phase-averaged profiles of one blade tip measured with DIC when the blade span is horizontal, and the tangential velocity is pointing downwards. Coordinates x, y are normalized by the chord length at the blade tip with origin at the quarter chord.

The measurements demonstrate the mechanism of the passive morphing concept. The undeformed flexible blade was designed with a significant initial camber, noticeably higher than that of the conventional rigid blade profile. The high camber present in both the initial blade shape and the subsequent deformed shape before reaching the designed operating point is the primary reason for the higher thrust force generated by the flexible blade operating off-design. Under hydrodynamic loading, the flexible trailing edge deflects upwards, causing the entire profile to flatten into a shape with less camber. This passive feathering becomes more pronounced with higher inflow velocities, which is the mechanism that reduces the thrust coefficient at high tip-speed ratios and velocities.

DIC measurements of different blades (Extended Data Figs. 1 and 2) show that blades with lower flexural rigidity undergo greater camber reduction and exhibit stronger load shedding. Specifically, for blades with the same mould geometry, a too-stiff blade results in a too-low pitch and too-high camber, and thus high mean and unsteady thrust. Conversely, a too-soft blade results in an over-pitched blade and low power capture.

The observed mean load-shedding behaviour shown in Fig. 1 arises primarily from quasi-steady passive morphing, and not from dynamic blade deformation resulting in hysteresis, vortex dynamics, and so on. DIC reconstructions of each individual blade at the same azimuthal position reveal only a narrow spread about the mean shape, corresponding to a standard deviation of the pitch variation of approximately ±0.2° (Extended Data Fig. 3).

To further verify that the mean load-shedding behaviour is due to a quasi-steady morphing, we compare the measured blade deformations (Fig. 4) and the corresponding power and thrust (Fig. 1) with those computed with an in-house fluid–structure interaction solver based on a quasi-steady low-order model (Methods). The blade shapes computed with this program are in good agreement with those measured experimentally, and so are the predicted power and thrust for different tip-speed ratios (Extended Data Fig. 4). Because the numerical solver assumes the blade is in static equilibrium under hydrodynamic loads, these results confirm that the governing physics is quasi-steady.

The fluid–structure interaction of the flexible blades is governed by two non-dimensional groups such as the Reynolds number (Re) and Cauchy number (Ca) (defined in the Methods). The experiments are performed at sufficiently high Re that the hydrodynamic load coefficients are about the same as those at full scale, as shown by the almost identical values for the rigid blade tested at different velocities in Fig. 1. To ensure geometric similarity between the model and the full-scale strain of the flexible blades, the Young modulus E of rubber must be scaled up to maintain the same Ca across scales. As discussed in Supplementary Note 4, rubber features a sufficiently high range of E for full-scale applications. Furthermore, rubber has the advantage of matching the mass density of water, enabling the design of buoyancy-neutral blades and preventing mass-related load fluctuations.

To demonstrate the scalability of the present results, numerical simulations are performed using the in-house fluid–structure interaction solver to model a utility-scale turbine. A rated speed of u∞ = 3.0 m s−1 and a 20-m diameter turbine is selected consistently with modern, state-of-the-art commercial turbines26 and typical energetic tidal sites27. Simulations performed at the respective Re and the same Ca confirm that power and thrust coefficient curves are similar at model and full scale (Extended Data Fig. 5), and therefore the present results are applicable to utility-scale turbines. Although E of the steel spar can be scaled up in numerical simulations, this is not possible in practice. Therefore, different full-scale spar design options are discussed in Supplementary Note 5.

Finally, rubber features high fatigue endurance. Preliminary calculations in Supplementary Note 6 show that the fatigue life of a full-scale rubber blade would substantially surpass the 20 years of service expected by state-of-the-art turbines.

Overall, by allowing similar control on power at thrust above rated speed than active pitch control systems, and mitigating load fluctuations, this technology offers a viable pathway to lower the LCOE. Furthermore, the reduction in load fluctuations enables deployment in energetic, highly turbulent sites previously deemed unviable due to the high fatigue loads. Further analysis of the potential industrial impact of this technology is presented in Supplementary Note 7.

This experimental investigation has evaluated the performance of tidal turbine flexible rubber blades with passive chordwise flexibility, compared against conventional rigid blades. Our results confirmed that the power coefficient of the flexible blade at the design tip-speed ratio is comparable to that of its rigid counterpart, demonstrating that load mitigation benefits are achieved without penalty to the primary function of the turbine as an energy harvester.

The main advantage of the flexible blades is their ability to deform, shedding the excess of load at off-design conditions. This reconfiguration allows control of power by manipulating the angular velocity of the turbine, while achieving passive mitigation of the high-frequency fluctuations that drive fatigue damage.

Therefore, the chordwise-flexible blades offer a compelling and robust alternative to state-of-the-art active pitch control. By mitigating loads with a much simpler setup, the flexible blade eliminates a significant source of potential failure and maintenance costs in offshore renewables.

The mechanism for load mitigation is confirmed through DIC measurement and a quasi-steady low-order code, which shows that the stiffness and initial geometry of the blade produce a controlled ‘feather’ as loads increase. The no-flow geometry and stiffness of the blade are designed so that, under flow conditions approaching the design point, it deforms toward the reference rigid-blade configuration.

Looking ahead, this work opens up new pathways for tidal turbine design and cost reduction. The demonstrated reductions in peak and fatigue loading could allow a reduction in structural requirements for both the blades and their supporting structure, lowering capital costs and enabling higher generator ratings, which in turn improve rated capacity per unit mass. Moreover, the increased robustness from the removal of the pitching system reduces operational and maintenance costs. These factors contribute to a lower LCOE of tidal turbines, addressing the primary barrier to the large-scale deployment of tidal energy farms. By making the technology more financially viable, this technology offers a realistic and attractive option for renewable energy production.

All experiments were conducted in the FloWave Ocean Energy Research Facility at the University of Edinburgh, a circular combined wave–current basin designed for scaled testing of offshore renewable energy devices. The tank has a diameter of 25 m and, for the present campaign, was operated in current-only mode with a working water depth of 1.92 m. A schematic of the facility is shown in Extended Data Fig. 6a. The experiments were performed at six inflow velocities in the range u∞ = 0.444–0.923 m s−1, corresponding to a diameter-based Reynolds number,

from 0.49 × 106 to 1.16 × 106, where ν is the kinematic viscosity and d is the turbine diameter. See Supplementary Note 4 for a discussion on the Reynolds number scaling.

FloWave turbulence is between 8% and 9%, and integral length scales of about 25% of the water depth28. These turbulent characteristics are consistent with energetic tidal sites such as, for example, the Fall of Warness29. There, the turbulence intensity is between 5% and 11%, with integral length scales of approximately 30–50% of the channel depth. The mean vertical shear in FloWave is approximately a power law with a 1/12 exponent (Extended Data Fig. 6b), which is only slightly weaker than the 1/10 power-law profile commonly used to represent tidal flows30. Extended Data Table 1 summarizes the comparison between FloWave and the representative tidal sites.

A three-bladed horizontal-axis turbine with a rotor diameter d = 1.26 m was installed in the tank centre, at hub height zhub = 0.876 m. The turbine is equipped with a brushless d.c. motor and a 25:1 planetary gearbox. The main components of the turbine are outlined in Extended Data Fig. 7.

The results presented in the main text refer to four sets of blades: one set of rigid blades used as a baseline and three sets of rubber blades. The baseline rigid blades are CNC-machined (SS316) using a modified NACA 63-415 hydrofoil profile along the span. The profile was modified to ensure a blunt trailing edge, as specified in ref. 31. These blades exhibited negligible flapwise and edgewise deformations. Notably, utility-scale tidal turbine blades exhibit some structural compliance. However, here the model-scale rigid blade was deliberately made rigid to provide a defined geometry.

The main text presents the results for the rigid blades and one set of rubber blades with the optimal stiffness. Conversely, the Extended Data figures also include results for the other two sets of rubber blades, with higher and lower stiffness than optimal. The flexible blades were manufactured by injecting a proprietary rubber mixture into a mould and around a steel spar. All rubber blades have the same mould geometry. See Extended Data Fig. 8 for schematics of the rubber blade. The aeroelastic properties of the blade are tailored along its span by varying the ratio of the rigid spar width to the local chord length, which increases from the tip towards the root with an average of 45%.

The thrust and torque are measured by a force transducer installed between the turbine rotor and the motor shaft (Extended Data Fig. 7). The transducer is bespoke, manufactured by Applied Measurements, rated for an axial load of 1,300 N and a torque of 100 N m, and a resolution of 0.005 N and 0.0004 N m, respectively. In this study, thrust is the net force measured by the hub transducer along the streamwise direction, and torque is the net edgewise moment about the hub axis. Moreover, each blade root was instrumented with a flapwise custom root-bending-moment sensor. Calibration matrices for each sensor were obtained in situ before the test by applying known weights at four points along the cantilever beam attached to the sensor. All force signals were transmitted to a National Instruments NI 9203 acquisition system through a slip ring. The load cells were zeroed without flow before each set of measurements. For each measurement, loads were recorded at a sampling frequency of 128 Hz for 300 s. Rotor angular velocity was measured using an inductive proximity sensor that emitted one pulse per blade pass (three pulses per revolution), enabling determination of the revolution period and computation of the angular velocity.

The principal measured quantities were torque (Q), thrust (T), flapwise root-bending moment (M) and angular velocity (ω). Measured loads and power are non-dimensionalized using standard turbine coefficients:

where ω is the turbine angular velocity in radians per second.

Sensor accuracy and calibration uncertainties were propagated to the non-dimensional coefficients using standard bias-limit uncertainty analysis32, including thrust-torque transducer manufacturer specification (0.1% of full-scale capacity) and primary uncertainties in u∞, ω and geometric parameters. For the present setup, the maximum total bias limits is of order 10−2 for CP and of order 10−2 for CT (representative values). Supplementary Note 1 provides the full derivations and tables.

Blade deformation was measured using phase-locked DIC with underwater cameras and LED illumination (LaVision). The camera system had a fixed focal length of 1.1 m and a field of view of approximately 0.87 m × 0.56 m, sufficient to capture the full blade span (0.56 m). Phase locking was achieved by using the proximity-sensor signal to trigger image acquisition as a blade passed a fixed azimuthal position, with a horizontal span and a downward tangential velocity. For each condition, between 89 and 447 instantaneous deformation fields were recorded over a 300 s period, depending on u∞ and λ.

Images were processed in LaVision DaVis 11 using a subset size of 21 × 21 pixels and a grid step size of 2 × 2 pixels, resulting in a spatial resolution of approximately 0.68 mm near the blade tip (approximately 2% of the tip chord). A reference image in quiescent water was acquired before each set of measurements. In the present configuration, DIC was used to measure the deformation of the suction-side surface of the blade. The full blade profile was reconstructed by combining the measured chord-line deformation with the known undeformed thickness distribution.

A bespoke fluid–structure interaction (FSI) solver was developed for the present study. The solver couples an in-house code based on blade element momentum theory (BEMT), with a panel method with an integral boundary-layer formulation (XFOIL), and a finite element analysis commercial software (Abaqus). The code uses a two-level iterative process, as schematically shown in Extended Data Fig. 9. The process begins with an initial blade geometry. In the outer loop, the BEMT solver is used to calculate the axial and tangential induction factors on a finite number of blade sections at different radial coordinates. Then, the flow velocity and angle of attack experienced by each blade section are computed. These values are used as initial conditions for the inner FSI loop. First, the pressure distributions around each blade section are computed with XFOIL. Then, the pressure distributions from each blade section are combined to obtain a three-dimensional pressure distribution on the blade, which is used as input to Abaqus, in which a new deformed shape is computed. The Abaqus model includes the steel spar. This new shape is then discretized into sections and returned to XFOIL to recalculate the pressure field. This iterative process continues until the blade shape converges. This deformed blade geometry at equilibrium is then fed back into the outer BEMT loop to update the induction factors. This entire two-level process is repeated until convergence. The power and thrust coefficients of the whole turbine are then computed by integrating the loads computed with XFOIL for each blade section and multiplying by three to account for the three-bladed turbine.

This code was used to design the stress-free mould shape for each blade stiffness, ensuring that the equilibrium blade shape matches the reference rigid blade at the design flow speed and tip-speed ratio. The model-scale simulations in Extended Data Figs. 4 and 5 are initialized with the mould geometry and use the actual stiffness of the metal spar and of the rubber. In the full-scale simulations (Extended Data Fig. 5), the stiffness of both the spar and the rubber is 10.6 times higher than at model scale to ensure that the model and full-scale Cauchy number for both the spar and the rubber is the same, where

where ρ is the fluid mass density and E is the Young’s modulus.

The data supporting the findings of this study are available at Edinburgh DataShare repository33.

The in-house fluid–structure interaction code (coupled BEMT, XFOIL and finite element analysis) used to design the blades and to generate the numerical results reported in this study is available at Edinburgh DataShare repository33.

The mould geometry Xi,j is used as input, where i = 0 and j = 0 indicate the iteration number of the inner and outer loop, respectively. The lift and drag coefficient curves (\({C}_{{{\rm{L}}}_{i,j}}(\alpha )\), \({C}_{{{\rm{D}}}_{i,j}}(\alpha )\)) are computed with XFOIL for various blade sections, and the induction factors (\({a}_{i,j},{a}_{i,j}^{{\prime} }\)) are computed with BEMT. Then the pressure distribution (pi,j(x)) around each blade section is computed with XFOIL and assembled into a three-dimensional load condition for Abaqus, where the new geometry is computed (Xi,j, with i increased by one). The inner loop is repeated till ∣∣Xi,j − Xi−1,j∣∣ is smaller than an acceptable threshold ϵi. If converged, the new geometry is Xi,j, where j is increased by one. The outer loop is repeated from the computation of the lift and drag coefficient for the new geometry, till ∣∣Xi,j − Xi,j−1∣∣ is smaller than an acceptable threshold ϵj.

#1536. Archie Gray and Hayden Hackney on Scotland's radar as Sebastien Pocognoli looks to tempt stars away from England

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:44 EST, 12 November 2026 | Updated: 17:53 EST, 12 November 2026

Sebastien Pocognoli has revealed that Scotland are stepping up their efforts to persuade players who are eligible for England to wear Dark Blue.

While the Belgian is content with the group of players at his disposal, he admits he and the SFA are in dialogue with certain individuals who, potentially, could improve the squad.

It’s understood that Tottenham’s Archie Gray and Everton’s Hayden Hackney are among the names with whom there are ongoing discussions ahead of the Euro 2028 qualifiers next year.

Both players have represented England – the country in which they were born – at Under-21 level yet could still switch to Scotland through family connections.

‘I have had direct contact or indirect contact,’ the Belgian admitted when asked about similarly eligible players. ‘When I go to the direct contact, it’s because I feel it’s a first positive approach.

‘Yeah, I’ve done it with many players. I’ll do my best to bring them.’

Scotland boss Pocognoli is keen to add to his options and has spoken to potential new recruits

Under Steve Clarke, Scotland tried to persuade Harvey Barnes to switch allegiance only for the Newcastle player to confirm that he felt English.

Prepared to take each case on its merits, Pocognoli explained: ‘With Barnes it was different. The two other lads (Gray and Hackney) are young lads. It’s a long way. But if you wait too long, it might not be the right moment.

‘In a year’s time, we will see. Right now, we have players in the squad who are performing well.

‘It will always be up to them (current players) to be the priority because we’ve built things and we’ve had time with the ones who are here right now.’

While Pocognoli has previously made it clear that he won’t beg any player to pull on a Scotland shirt, he feels it’s incumbent on him and the SFA to gauge the feelings of players down south who could help his side.

‘We are on it,’ he stressed. ‘We are always proactive in all of these situations.

‘What is very exciting about those two names is that they are young players. That’s interesting.

Archie Gray's dad Andy, uncle Eddie and grandfather Frank all represented Scotland

‘We have to look and manage the situation. But it won’t be a definitive choice from them because we weren’t proactive. That has to be clear. We are proactive.

‘The best way to convince players is to show good football, show them they can come to us, enjoy it and be successful. They have to feel when they leave a top club that they arrive here into top conditions and a top environment.

‘That’s the best publicity we can offer, to show good football. In the end, it’s a human decision, a feeling.

‘I didn’t have that case. With my Italian blood, maybe I wasn’t that good! But I can understand the feeling of what it’s like to have to choose a country, with your background, family, football education and social circle.

‘So, it’s not easy. But it’s always a feeling from inside and I need to feel it. When I feel it, I’ll try to be on it.’

Hayden Hackney has impressed for Everton this season and has played for Scotland Under-21s

Meanwhile, Pocognoli believes a fully fit Kieran Tierney can have a major role to play in his new-look side.

While the preferred systems of his predecessors meant accommodating the Celtic man and Andy Robertson could be a conundrum, the 3-4-3 which the Belgian deploys seems better suited to fielding the pair at the same time.

With Tierney back in contention to face North Macedonia after pulling out of the last squad through injury, the manager said: ‘He will bring a different profile. He has a fantastic left foot and is an experienced player who knows the squad and knows what it means to play for Scotland. It is a big plus. He trained very well this week and is very focused.

‘He can play different positions. He can play left-back, he can play in the back three, as he has in the past. He plays left-back for Celtic, but in some games he has inverted. He can also bring some offensive attributes in the back three. We are lucky to have someone with that profile.

‘It is always a challenge to try to make all the players shine in the best shape possible. We have strong competition on the left side.

‘We have quality players. I will try to find the best balance and make everybody shine. If we can play Kieran and Andy in the same team if they are fit, it is a plus for the team.’

Kieran Tierney has been tipped to have a big impact for Scotland under Pocognoli

Pocognoli is desperate to secure his first victory at Hampden this evening having tasted defeat in his first two home games with Switzerland and Slovenia.

‘I haven’t really experienced Hampden yet and I’d like to,’ he said. ‘I was frustrated in the first game (against the Swiss) because I thought we started quite good in the first 10 minutes.

‘Then we know what happened (red card for Jack Hendry). In the last game, it was just disappointment.

‘It’s important that we play a consistent game and combine a good result with good football. If we play average and win, I’ll be happy with three points.

‘But the process is to play good football as well. It’s important that we excite the fans and we have the players for that. I hope that we deliver what we’ve worked on in the last four days.’

#1535. Andoni Iraola: Liverpool cannot ‘sustain the level’ I want

Andoni Iraola has conceded that Liverpool cannot currently “sustain the level” he expects after his side squandered a two-goal lead for the second match in a row.

In the Spaniard’s first game at Anfield since becoming manager, Monaco fought back to win 3-2 by virtue of Paris Brunner’s late glancing header seven days on from Leeds United’s 4-2 victory in Chicago, emphasising Liverpool’s alarming lack of depth, particularly in defence.

“We played a good first half, especially a good 30 minutes. Right now we probably don’t have much more, in terms of the levels required to play like this. They deserved to turn around the game.

“We won the first two pre-season games, but the last two we cannot sustain the level we want for all of the game. As soon as we made some changes, players start to get tired and we cannot sustain that level. So, we have work to do.”

Alex on target 🎯 pic.twitter.com/PT6AYrLxyz

Alisson, Virgil van Dijk and Cody Gakpo all made their first appearances and contributed to a lively first-half in which Iraola’s commitment to man-to-man marking and an intensive pressing structure were evident out of possession. With the ball in the first half they demonstrated the kind of slick passing that Bournemouth employed to carve opponents open on the counter-attack.

A nimble one-two between Ryan Gravenberch and Dominik Szoboszlai allowed the Dutch midfielder to set up Alexander Isak to score with a shot from 16 yards and the most expensive player in English football history laid claim to the second, too, when he seemed to hook in a rebound from Lukas Hradecky’s save while lying in the six-yard box.

Later he would graciously acknowledge that he and Florian Wirtz had connected with the ball simultaneously and he was happy to yield the credit to his team-mate.

Our second goal of the game, scored by Wirtz… we think 🤔 pic.twitter.com/FUzA363Oxw

At that point it seemed that victory would be a cakewalk but just before half-time Aleksandr Golovin caught Van Dijk out with a feint and late swerve to the right, tripping over the Liverpool captain’s clumsy hack. Despite a heavy limp, Golovin hammered the penalty past Alisson’s dive to make it 2-1 at the break.

Iraola rationed his early changes at the start of the second half to two but Liverpool could not regain their rhythm and Mika Biereth capitalised on a Gravenberch error to score the equaliser after battling to be first to the rebound when Giorgi Mamardashvili saved his first effort, stroking his effort through Wataru Endo’s legs.

Cue five substitutions as soon as that goal had gone in and a raft more followed, killing the remaining half-hour of all momentum and cohesion. By the time Brunner exploited a dozy mix-up between Milos Kerkez and Federico Chiesa about whose responsibility he was at a corner to flash his header past Mamardashvili, only two of the 22 starters were still on the pitch.

Liverpool: Alisson (Mamardashvili 46), Tsimikas (Kerkez 59), Van Dijk (c) (Chambers 59), Ndukwe (Endo 46), Frimpong (Ramsay 75), Gravenberch (Nyoni 59), Gakpo (Ngumoha 59), Wirtz (McConnell 59), Koumas (Chiesa 75), Isak (Muñoz 59)Substitutes: Morrison, Davies.Goals: Isak (16), Wirtz (29)Monaco: Hradecky, Nazinho (Mawissa 75), Dier (c) (Kehrer 75), S Sané, Vanderson (Teze 46), Golovin (Idumbo 75), Cabral (Soubeir 75), Camara (Benzahra 64), Detourbet (Coulibaly 64), Biereth (Brunner 80), Abline (Konaté 64).Substitutes: Assab, Kohn, Lienard, Nibombe, Touré.  Goals: Golovin (44 pen), Biereth (56), Brunner (88)

They played well in the first half, as they did against Leeds, but lost all shape and structure in the second half to lose 3-2.

Yellow card for Konate for clattering into Endo late. That’s the last of the action.

Liverpool 2 Monaco 3 (Brunner)  Brilliant near-post glancing header from a devilishly whippy, dipping corner. Kerkez doing his best Rip van Winkle impression.

Diligent defensive work by Ngumoha stops Konate’s run down the outside left.

A final substitution, hopefully. Brunner replaces Biereth. Konate’s shot, a pearoller, is easily saved by Mamardashvili after A mix-up between Kerkez and Munoz.

As usual, the substitutions have killed the game. Watched Leeds vs RB Leipzig yesterday. They played two 60 minute matches which kept it more competitive for longer but still descended into a kickabout late on.

Mawissa, Kehrer, Idumbo and Soubeir have replaced Nazinho, Dier, Golovin and Cabral.

Monaco also made changes, four I think. Will catch up with then once they’re confirmed. Ramsey is into the game straight away tp stop Coulibaly’s shot.

Ramsay, Chiesa and Elliott are coming on for Szoboszlai, Frimpong and Koumas. Lovely applause for Elliott.

Konate sweeps a left-foot shot from the left of the box past the right post with Mamardashvili forced into a headlong dive. Liverpool have lost their defensive shape and intensity, allowing Monaco to punch holes through the lines with some direct running.

Nazinho gets round Frimpong down the Monaco left and cuts back the perfect pass to put it on a plate for Coulibaly who hammers a left-foot shot from the right of the D that Mamardashvili throws up his hands to block. That would have stung. Good save. A flag would have meant it wouldn’t have counted but even so Frimpong’s defensive work wasn’t good enough.

It’s been very scrappy since the changes but then Ngumoha pounces on to a loose ball, glides up the right and tries to play Koumas in behind the back four. Sadly, he overhits the pass which trickles out for a goal-kick. Cue an ovation and cries of ‘Rio! Rio!’

Three changes for Monaco with Detoubet, Abline and Camara departing for Benzhara, Coulibaly and Konaté.

Ngumoha has gone to the right wing and Koumas is playing through the middle as a false nine.

Liverpool make five changes with Gakpo, Van Dijk, Wirtz, Tsimikas and Isak departing while Munoz makes his ‘debut’ with Ngumoha, Nyoni, Chambers, McConell and Kerkez.

Liverpool 2 Monaco 2 (Biereth) Mistake by Gravenberch allows Golovin to play a pass into the left half of the box for Biereth. His first shot is well saved by Mamardashvili at full stretch but his tenacity allowed him to get to the rebound ahead of Endo, swivel and stick his second effort in to equalise.

Monaco overplay at the edge of the box, Detourbet, Biereth and Abline playing ‘after you. Claud’, instead of shooting.

A slick, short passing move between Gravenberch, Wirtz and Isak ends with Isak on the deck in the box after Gravenberch’s step-over allowed the ball to run to him. Isak took a touch to move the ball on to his left but gave the defender a glimmer of it and he hacked it away before felling Isak as well as collateral damage.

Quiet start to the half. Biereth just pressed Mamardashvili but the keeper managed to sweep the ball away even though under more pressure than he would have expected.

Liverpool try to play out from the back with Mamardashvili spearing a straight pass to Gravenberch who tried to knock it round the corner for Endo but the ball skidded under his studs and out for a throw-in.

Isak is apparently claiming both goals. Replays are indistinct. He could have clipped it in off his heel as he had a swing at the ball while grounded at the same time as Wirtz.

Our second goal of the game, scored by Wirtz… we think 🤔 pic.twitter.com/FUzA363Oxw

Endo has slotted in at centre-back alongside Van Dijk.

Half-time changes: Mamardashvili for Alisson and Endo for Ndukwe.

For Monaco, Teze for Vanderson at right-back.

Much to admire in that first-half performance from Liverpool’s front six and centre-backs, the latter two particularly out of possession and winning it back. The man-to-man system is working well for them. But they should be out of sight by now instead of leading by only a goal.

Liverpool free-kick on the right after a foul on Koumas. Szoboszlai whips in the cross and Van Dijk gets up first to the left of the penalty spot but bludgeons his header about a foot wide of the right post.

Charlie Adam says the penalty was ‘a soft one’ but Van Dijk did not adjust when Golovin shifted it to his right, stuck out a leg and Golovim understandably decided to topple over the hurdle.

Liverpool 2 Monaco 1 (Golovin, pen) Speared it into the top right. Alisson went the right way but was beaten for pace and power.

The referee, Jarred Gillett, gives Monaco a penalty. It was deserved, too. Golovin went on a driving run down the middle, shifted it to his right and was tripped by Van Dijk.

Liverpool are well worth their lead. They are streets ahead of Monaco.

A microcosm of the game so far: Liverpool pass goes astray, a player wins it back – this time Gakpo – by snapping into a tackle before laying it off to his left for the unmarked Tsimikas to skim a low shot about a foot wide of the left post from 25 yards.

Monaco have done very little since that wee salvo in the opening minute but just now Abline was given too much space from distance but whacked his shot into the Kop.

Big cheer from the crowd for Hugo Ekitike

The impressive Koumas diddles Nazinho with a Cruyff turn but then thumps his shot straight into Hradecky’s chest.

Liverpool 2 Monaco 0 (Wirtz) Pass chipped out to Koumas down the right who arcs a cross to the back post. Gakpo meets it with a header back across goal to Isak whose first effort from a couple of yards is blocked but the ball gets stuck under Isak’s falling body and Wirtz is Johnny on the Spot to stab it in from a 18 inches as Dier tried to scramble it away.

Liverpool have been impressive so far but if there has been a weakness it’s still the balance in central midfield defensively. Going forward both Gravenberch and Szobiszlai have dovetailed together well. They win the ball back when Van Dijk steps out and the midfield two fly forward to tee up Koumas for a shot that strikes Dier.

Chance for Wirtz, who opens his body from the left of the D to try to bend a shot into the bottom right corner but fizzes it the wrong side of the post.

It’s been pretty breathless since the goal, Liverpool dozily letting Monaco through the middle before twice cutting Monaco apart in midfield only for Isak to overrun a pass in the box delivered by Wirtz and then Koumas to shoot over.

Liverpool 1 Monaco 0 (Isak) Chip to Gakpo down the left of the box, he clips it first time back to Gravenberch in the D who lays it off to Szoboszlai. Ping-ping-ping. Szoboszlai keeps the tempo high with return, the one in the one-two with Gravenberch who picks out Isak to bury a shot from about 15 yards into the bottom left corner.

Alex on target 🎯 pic.twitter.com/PT6AYrLxyz

Excellent move from Liverpool, instigated by Ndukwe’s fine tackle on Biereth. He knocks it short to Gravenberch who arrows a 60-yard pass out to Koumas hurtling down the right. He measures his cross perfectly for Gakpo stealing in off the left wing and though he connects powerfully with the meat of his brow, he bashes it straight at the keeper. He was offside in any case, it transpires.

Charlie Adam on co-comms points out that Liverpool are going man-to-man now in classic Iraola/Bielsa style and when the camera goes high you can see it, especially with the full-backs.

Liverpool are carving the middle of the park up with incisive passing. Szoboszlai starts a move that sends Isak down the left of the box. He traps the chip, turns back to face away from goal and taps a pass back to Wirtz who gallops on to it and bends a shot that Hradecky dives low to his left to beat away with a firm left wrist. Frimpong pounces on the rebound and clips a tame effort straight at Hradecky who had quickly restored himself to the vertical.

Van Dijk gobbles up a long pass over Ndukwe, snuffing out any possibility of Biereth getting there first.

Tsimikas is free down the left but overhits his cross on the run when Isak was begging for a cut-back. The left-back went for the back post and ballooned his centre behind, miles beyond Koumas and Wirtz.

Liverpool defend the corner solidly and Frimpong races away on the counter, bombing on to the ball and sprinting into the Monaco half. But his touch is not as sound as his pace and Monaco deal with him when he fluffs his control.

A period of applause in memory of Kevin Keegan ❤️ pic.twitter.com/AkPZG7babe

Liverpool kick off defending the Kop. They roll the ball back to Frimpong who chips a long pass up the right to Koumas who hares on to the pass down the right and crosses, just beyond Isak. Hradecky gathers and bowls the ball out. A mistake by Tisimikas lets Biereth barrel through the inside-right to hammer a shot that Alisson turns behind for a corner.

The crowd applauds in the modern way. My goodness he was a terrific player. Saw him play for Liverpool, Southampton and Newcastle. Absolutely relentless.

Virgil van Dijk has the pennant. Liverpool are wearing all red with the paint splashes of the 1990 kit. Monaco are in a very pale green.

For me it’s a special game, most of the players and people will be ‘it’s [just] a pre-season friendly’, but for me it’s a lot more than this. It will be the first time I have the chance to go out, to feel this stadium and I hope we can also perform well.

It’s a good game for us, because it’s going to be demanding, it’s a team that wants to dominate and they also want to press high so we will see how we are.

I think the cases of Ali[sson], Cody, and Virgil I think it’s their first game. It shouldn’t go longer than 45 minutes, maybe a little bit more if they feel comfortable.

Also for some of the others Ryan, Flo, and Alex, it’s the second game so we have to be aware of those things.

But the league starts in two weeks, so we cannot wait also too much; we have to give them quality minutes.

I think today is going to be a good reference, two games – Monaco and Como – teams that try dominate the game, they are very good in possession, so they will demand us the best without the ball. If we want to control the game and also physical teams, they are probably a very good test.

I hope we are at the level and we can do very good games.

Liverpool Alisson; Frimpong, Ndukwe, Van Dijk, Tsimikas; Szoboszlai, Gakpo; Koumaz, Wirtz, Gakpo; Isak.

Monaco Hradecky; Vanderson, Dier, Sané, Nazinho; Detourbet, Cabral, Camara, Golovin, Abline, Biereth.

Le 𝐗𝐈 qui débutera cette rencontre face à 𝐋𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐩𝐨𝐨𝐥 📋 pic.twitter.com/2cOYRbzUEN

🥳 Feliz aniversário, 𝐅𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐩𝐞 𝐋𝐮𝐢́𝐬! 🎉Notre coach fête aujourd'hui ses 41 ans 🎂 pic.twitter.com/VTd4BQ5rRK

Alisson, Van Dijk and Gakpo return, Ndukwe continues in defence.

The Reds to take on AS Monaco at Anfield!Watch the match LIVE on All Red Video 📺

Good afternoon and welcome to live coverage of the first of two Liverpool home friendlies after their preseason tour of the United States. Andoni Iraola’s side saw off Wrexham and Sunderland in their first two matches but gave away a two-goal lead at half-time in the final fixture and ended up being beaten 4-2 by Leeds United in Chicago in the last game after multiple changes. What did we learn? Not a huge amount in the absence of Virgil van Dijk, Alisson, Víctor Muñoz, Cody Gakpo and Alexis Mac Allister, the first four of whom are available today other than an ongoing vulnerability from set-pieces and Curtis Jones looking like he is in desperate need of a fresh start.

This afternoon at Anfield they take on AS Monaco who finished seventh in Ligue 1 this season but are under new management with the recruitment of the former Chelsea and Atlético left-back Filipe Luís as head coach. It’s quite the coup for Le Rocher given he led Flamengo to their first Brazilian title in five years, the Copa Libertadores and the Copa do Brasil in his 18 months in charge.

In pre-season so far he has overseen a 5-2 win over fourth-tier AS Saint-Priest, a 2-0 defeat by Sporting Clube, a 2-2 draw with Cercle Bruges and a 1-0 victory over Getafe. They have sold their best player, Maghnes Akliouche, to PSG for £43m and Aladji Bamba to Newcastle for £34m but have so far retained Mamadou Coulibaly and Folarin Balogun, signed and made Ansu Fati’s loan move into a long-term deal.

Iraola may well persevere with Trey Nyoni in midfield who, after his performances on tour, ought to be on the threshold of a breakthrough season and it would be interesting to see him paired with Ryan Gravenberch just behind Dominik Szoboszlai.

Ifeanyi Ndukwe, who played well in America after coming on for the injured Joe Gomez, does not have a UK work permit and will have to go abroad on loan for the season but Jérémy Jacquet, who has yet to feature, was due to have a fitness test this morning and would be a welcome to boost to a squad whose defence still requires significant reinforcements.
