#1533. Arsenal lose second successive pre-season friendly after parading Guimaraes

Arsenal suffered back-to-back pre-season defeats as they lost 3-2 to Borussia Dortmund in the Emirates Cup on Sunday.

The loss to the German side followed a 3-1 defeat by Real Betis on Wednesday night in Dublin.

Before kick-off, Bruno Guimarães was paraded to the Arsenal faithful after completing his £75m move from Newcastle on Saturday.

But enthusiasm about the Brazilian’s arrival was dampened when Dortmund took the lead at the Emirates inside the opening 10 minutes. Felix Nmecha’s incisive pass into the penalty area was met by the run of Samuele Inácio, who made no mistake with a clinical finish into the far corner.

The Bundesliga side doubled their lead just before the half-hour mark as 18-year-old Greek international Konstantinos Karetsas curled one in from the edge of the box.

Ten minutes after half-time, Arsenal pulled a goal back through Ethan Nwaneri, who scored from Christos Tzolis’s cross. However, moments later Dortmund restored their two-goal advantage as Joane Gadou smashed home from a corner.

Arsenal kept their hopes alive through a Viktor Gyokeres penalty after Tzolis was brought down, but Dortmund were able to hold on to claim victory. After the full-time whistle, there was a penalty shoot-out, which Arsenal won 5-4.

Arsenal still have a number of players to return to action following their World Cup exploits, including Declan Rice, Bukayo Saka and Noni Madueke. England and Real Madrid midfielder Jude Bellingham was in attendance at the Emirates to watch his younger brother Jobe in action for Dortmund.

As well as Guimarães, there was another addition on display at the Emirates: Arsenal have added last year’s title win to the list of honours displayed inside the stadium.

Arsenal play Cesc Fàbregas’s Como on Wednesday, before taking on Manchester City in the Community Shield next weekend. Mikel Arteta’s side then start the defence of their Premier League crown at home against newly promoted Coventry City.

Arsenal: Kepa (Meslier 46); White (Julienne 78), Mosquera (Ogunnaike 78), Gabriel (Salmon 60), Calafiori (Hincapié 60); Lewis-Skelly (Vieira 78), Havertz (O’Neill 78), Odegaard (Nwaneri 33); Dowman (Ibrahim 78), Gyokeres (Jesus 78), Tzolis (Martinielli 78). Substitutes: Setford, Nelson, Kabia.Booked: Gabriel.Goals: Nwaneri (54), Gyokeres (69 pen).Borussia Dortmund: Meyer; Svensson (Yamamoto 91), Inácio (Prates 59), Bensebaini (Reggiani 78), Gadou; Bellingham, Nmecha (Guirassy 60), Mane; Karetsas (Chukwuemeka 46), Beier (Sabitzer 59), Silva (Albert 59). Substitutes: Drewes, Lerema, Kabar, Riedl.Goals: Inácio (7), Karetsas (29), Gadou (58).

Nwaneri steps up with the chance to win the shootout and does so with aplomb, sending Meyer the wrong way, and Arsenal win the shootout 5-4.

The former Chelsea man receives some boos as he steps up but calmly slots home to keep Dortmund’s hopes alive.

Meyer goes the right way but there is far too much power on this penalty from Martinelli. Meyer had no chance of saving that one.

We have the first penalty miss of this shootout as Meslier guesses the right way and saves what was a pretty poor penalty from Albert. Advantage Arsenal.

A few stutters in the run-up but Hincapie slots home into the bottom left corner, with Meyer going the wrong way.

He came on right at the end of the game to take a penalty and rewards the decision from his manager to do so as he lifts it over Meslier diving to his left.

Another penalty scored in the left corner. Meyer again guesses the right way but cannot prevent Vieira.

There is a bit of a stutter in the run-up as Reggiani stares down Meslier and sends the Arsenal keeper the wrong way, finding the same corner as Sabitzer and Jesus.

Meyer in the Dortmund goal guesses the right way but Jesus lifts it over him with a quality penalty.

Meslier takes an age to get ready but Sabitzer does not care, sending the Arsenal keeper the wrong way and emphatically finding the left corner.

Right, we are ready for penalties. Dortmund will take first, with Sabitzer to take their opening penalty up against Meslier.

Arsenal have the ball in the net in the final few seconds and think they have a very late equaliser but Martinelli’s effort is ruled out for an offside. Meyer will be a relieved man in the Dortmund goal as he allowed Martinelli’s shot to go through him.

The final whistle is then blown and Dortmund have beaten Arsenal 3-2 to take the Emirates Cup.

It is perhaps not a massive surprise but the game has lost some flow with all the changes both sides have made during this second half.

There is set to be a penalty shootout at the end of this one, no matter what the final result is.

Former Arsenal midfielder Cesc Fabregas is in attendance, with his Como side taking on Arsenal here on Wednesday.

Jude Bellingham is supporting his younger brother Jobe today at the Emirates:

With just under 15 minutes to go at the Emirates, Arsenal are going to make a number of changes. Plenty of youngsters are entering the fray as are a few experienced players like Jesus and Martinelli.

The Swede sends Meyer the wrong way and slots into the bottom right corner. It is now 3-2 and this game is not over with 20 minutes to go.

Tzolis goes down inside the Dortmund penalty area and referee Chris Kavanagh points to the spot. He was caught inside the box and there did not appear to be too many complaints from the visitors.

Nwaneri comes close to getting his second goal of the half. Tzolis rolls it across the face of the penalty area to Nwaneri, who hits it first time and forces Meyer into a good save to his right, pushing it onto the post.

In the aftermath of that Dortmund goal, there are a raft of changes for both sides. Arsenal have brought on Salmon and Hincapie for Calafiori and Gabriel.

Dortmund have brought on the experience of the likes of Sabitzer and Guirassy.

Arsenal had some problems from corners the other day against Betis and they concede minutes after getting a goal back. Arsenal fail to deal with a corner from the right and the ball ends up with Gadou at the back post. Gadou takes one touch before finding the net, despite the best efforts of numerous Arsenal defenders on the line.

Should Inacio have gone down? The young Italian is played in behind the Arsenal defence and has Calafiori all over his back. Inacio ends up losing possession on the edge of the Arsenal penalty area but had he gone down Calafiori could have been in trouble.

Mikel Arteta’s side reduce Dortmund’s lead to just the one goal. Tzolis cuts it back from the left side of the box and picks out Nwaneri eight yards out from goal in the centre of the box. Nwaneri makes no mistake, smashing home and Arsenal are back in this game.

That is good defending from Nwaneri. Just as Chukwuemeka was lining up a shot just outside the box, Nwaneri tracks back and steals it off Chukwuemeka.

White is found on the right side of the box but is denied by Meyer in the Dortmund goal. The subsequent corner comes to nothing.

Dortmund are not far off scoring their third a couple of minutes into this second half. The ball is rolled into the feet of Nmecha outside the box. The German midfielder, who scored a stunner for his country against Curacao at the World Cup, nearly picks out the top corner but it goes just over Meslier’s bar.

Dortmund have brought on former Chelsea and Aston Villa man Chukwuemeka on at the break. Arsenal have made an alteration at the break with Meslier replacing Kepa in goal.

During half-time at the Emirates, the official song of the 2026 Fifa World Cup Dai Dai by Shakira and Burna Boy is being belted out over the tannoy. The World Cup final was exactly three weeks ago today, with three of Arsenal’s players in Spain’s winning squad; David Raya, Mikel Merino and Martin Zubimendi.

Konstantinos Karetsas has arrived. 🇬🇷🇬🇷🇬🇷 pic.twitter.com/nI4A7KPT4o

The first half in north London is brought to an end and it is the visitors Borussia Dortmund who lead 2-0 at the break courtesy of goals from Inacio and Karetsas.

Gabriel is into the book. He is in possession but his touch allows the ball to slightly get away from him. He then slides in to try and retain possession and catches Karetsas.

Two added minutes at the end of this first half.

Nmecha eyes up a repeat of Dortmund’s first goal as he tries to find the run of Inacio into the Arsenal box but this time they cannot quite link up.

After Gyokeres was fouled, Arsenal have a free-kick inside the Dortmund half. Tzolis clips it in and picks out Havertz in space inside the Dortmund box but the German is a fair way out from goal and his header is easily saved by Meyer.

Arsenal want a penalty but the appeals are turned down. It all stems from good work defensively from Tzolis, who drives forward from the edge of his own box and then finds Gyokeres out to his left. Tzolis continues his run into the Dortmund half and is found. Tzolis then finds Gyokeres again, who goes down inside the Dortmund penalty area after a challenge from Gadou but the Swedish striker went down far too easily and that is never a penalty.

Dowman does brilliantly down Arsenal’s right to get past Beier but then goes down just before the byline. Referee Chris Kavanagh blows his whistle and Beier cannot believe it. Replays show that Dowman threw himself to the ground and it was a dive.

Tzolis takes the free-kick and delivers it to the far post, where Gabriel meets it but his powerful header goes over the bar. The Brazilian probably should have scored.

Mikel Arteta has made a change as Nwaneri has replaced Odegaard, who has only recently returned to training after the World Cup.

With it being a warm day in north London, we have a water break. Hopefully they do not catch on after the World Cup. Mikel Arteta is looking pretty animated talking to his side.

What a finish that is to put the German side 2-0 up! 18-year-old Karetsas, who has joined Dortmund from Genk this summer, is afforded too much space outside the Arsenal penalty area as he drives towards the box and punishes the hosts for that, curling a sublime shot into the far corner.

Odegaard slides a clever pass into the right channel to pick out the run of Gyokeres towards the Dortmund box. Mane though slides in with a perfectly-timed challenge to take it off Gyokeres. Mane had to time that right with the challenge being right on the edge of his own box.

Arsenal hit the bar. Dowman does well down Arsenal’s right to drive into the Dortmund box and cuts it back to Gyokeres. The Swedish striker takes a few touches before getting his shot away, which clips the top of the bar.

A dangerous cross from the left comes all the way to Svensson at the back post but he lacked conviction with his header and it goes wide. Perhaps he should be hitting the target.

Down at the other end Arsenal have a headed chance of their own. Havertz clips in a cross from the left and picks out Gyokeres. The Swede is a fair way out from goal and his header goes wide.

Should Havertz have done better with this opportunity? The German is played in down the right channel and has Gyokeres calling for the cross in space in the centre of the box. Havertz tries to find him but Meyer is out to smother it. Had Havertz found Gyokeres, it would likely have been a simple tap-in for the Swede.

Odegaard appears to be through one-on-one but then goes down just outside the Dortmund box. Mane pleads his innocence but referee Chris Kavanagh does not agree, giving a free-kick. If this was a competitive game, Mane would potentially have been sent off.

Gyokeres will take and opts for power over accuracy. It is safe to say his effort is terrible, blazing over the bar and missing the target by some margin.

Calafiori trips Bellingham as Dortmund attempted to counter. If this was a competitive fixture, Calafiori likely would have been booked for that foul.

Bellingham and Havertz are involved in quite the collision. Both players go for the header and Havertz just gets to it first. Havertz is awarded the foul and is ok.

The German side take the lead inside the opening seven minutes. Nmecha slides a lovely pass through the Arsenal defensive line to pick out the run of Inacio into the Arsenal penalty area. It is a clinical finish from Inacio, who slides his effort into the far corner,

Dortmund’s first proper foray forward causes Arsenal issues and Tzolis is forced to put it behind for Dortmund’s first corner of the game. The inswinger though to the front post is poor and Gyokeres easily heads away from danger.

Gyokeres wins Arsenal their first corner of the game out on the right. Odegaard’s delivery into the near post causes problems for Dortmund and forces Dortmund keeper Meyer to tip over his own bar for another Arsenal corner. Meyer this time punches Odegaard’s delivery away and Dortmund clear their lines.

Moments after Bruno Guimaraes’ unveiling, both sides now emerge from the tunnel and we are moments away from kick-off at the Emirates.

Just before the two sides emerge the tunnel, there is a special guest who comes out first in the form of Bruno Guimaraes. Chants of “Bruno! Bruno!” ring around the Emirates as the Arsenal fans get their first glimpse of him in an Arsenal shirt, although the Brazilian is not involved today.

Arsenal: Kepa; White, Mosquera, Gabriel, Calafiori; Lewis-Skelly, Havertz, Odegaard; Dowman, Gyokeres, Tzolis.Substitutes: Meslier, Setford, Hincapie, Jesus, Martinielli, Vieira, Nwaneri, Nelson, Ibrahim, Kabia, Ogunnaike, Julienne, O’Neill, Salmon.

Borussia Dortmund: Meyer; Svensson, Inacio, Bensebaini, Gadou; Bellingham, Nmecha, Mane; Karetsas, Beier, Silva.Substitutes: Drewes, Guirassy, Chukwuemeka, Sabitzer, Lerema, Prates, Albert, Kabar, Yamamoto, Reggiani, Riedl.

Reports are that Jobe’s older brother Jude is at the Emirates today, not that Arsenal fans should think that Jude is swapping Real Madrid for the red half of north London.

Arsenal took the Premier League trophy with them to Dublin on Wednesday night and it is on show today at the Emirates. They kick off the defence of their crown on opening night against newly-promoted Coventry is just under two weeks.

Counting down until kick-off ⏰ Make sure you're in your seats by 1.45pm (UK), Gooners - we have a very special guest in store 👀

When Bruno Guimarães signed for Newcastle United from Lyon in January 2022, much was made of the idea that he had rejected Arsenal in favour of a move to St James’ Park. The Brazilian played along with it, posting a video on his social media pages which featured multiple newspaper headlines about Arsenal wanting to buy him.

The Newcastle fans, still delirious about the recent takeover by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, understandably lapped it up. Their dream was to overthrow the established powers in English football, and the capture of Guimarães was regarded as a sign that they were truly ready to challenge teams of Arsenal’s stature and wealth.

Even the lyrics to the midfielder’s chant referred to the north Londoners, as Newcastle fans sang that Guimarães “could have signed for Arsenal” but chose instead to play “in the famous black and white”.

Yesterday Arsenal announced the signing of Brazilian midfielder Bruno Guimaraes from Newcastle for £75m on a four-year deal, with the option of a further year. Here is what the Brazilian had to say:

“I feel good, I feel amazing. I am glad for the opportunity. Since the first time I spoke to (Andrea) Berta and Mikel (Arteta) I was excited. I just felt inside of me that I need a new challenge in my life and I think to be an Arsenal player is going to be an exciting challenge in my life.

“I think after playing two World Cups, I am at the point of my life, I think I need a challenge like this. I want to win trophies, I want to make history and I think I am in the right place to do it. I am so excited to start. We have tough games to play this season so the squad is going to be very, very important and I am hopeful we can achieve our dreams.”

Arsenal: Kepa; White, Mosquera, Gabriel, Calafiori; Lewis-Skelly, Havertz, Odegaard; Dowman, Gyokeres, Tzolis.Substitutes: Meslier, Setford, Hincapie, Jesus, Martinielli, Vieira, Nwaneri, Nelson, Ibrahim, Kabia, Ogunnaike, Julienne, O’Neill, Salmon.

Borussia Dortmund: Meyer; Svensson, Inacio, Bensebaini, Gadou; Bellingham, Nmecha, Mane; Karetsas, Beier, Silva.Substitutes: Drewes, Guirassy, Chukwuemeka, Sabitzer, Lerema, Prates, Albert, Kabar, Yamamoto, Reggiani, Riedl.

INS:Illan Meslier from Leeds, FreeChristos Tzolis from Club Brugge, £34mBruno Guimaraes from Newcastle, £75m

Piero Hincapie’s move from Bayer Leverkusen was made permanent this summer.

OUTS:Leandro Trossard to Besiktas, £18mJakub Kiwior to Porto, £15m

🚨 STARTING XI VS ARSENAL 🚨 pic.twitter.com/Wk6QPOGDnW

🔴 𝗧𝗘𝗔𝗠𝙉𝙀𝙒𝙎 ⚪️🧱 Gabriel at the back©️ Odegaard skippers the side😤 Gyokeres leads the line More pre-season minutes in the tank - let's do this, Gunners ✊🤝 Presented by @deel pic.twitter.com/FQwOjCDAje

Checking in for the Emirates Cup 🛬 pic.twitter.com/mQ1eAESKHY

Premier League champions Arsenal continue their preparations for the new season as they take on Borussia Dortmund in the Emirates Cup. Arsenal beat Spanish side Athletic Bilbao 3-0 in the 2025 edition, with goals from Viktor Gyokeres, Bukayo Saka and Kai Havertz sealing victory. These sides met during the 2014/15 Champions League group stages, with both games being won 2-0 by the home side.

Arsenal beat Girona 4-1 just over a week ago but fell to a 3-1 defeat to Real Betis in Dublin on Wednesday night. Reflecting on that defeat, Mikel Arteta expressed his frustration at the way his side conceded the goals.

“I am disappointed with the result,” Arteta told Arsenal’s in-house media. “We are here to win football matches. We had some fantastic moments in the first half, the way we played, the way we opened them up. We have to score first, clearly, in the two chances that we had before the score.

“I am very disappointed in the manner that we conceded the first goal, the two giveaways leading to the other two goals. It is true that the finishing quality from them was exceptional, but to win a football match, you have to compete at a different level, especially in those areas of the pitch and that is the learning from today [last Wednesday].”

This is in fact Arsenal’s first game at the Emirates since being crowned Premier League champions, as they sealed the title with a game to spare, with that final match of last season being away at Crystal Palace. After today, Arsenal have two more games, including the Community Shield in a week’s time, before they kick off the defence of their Premier League crown at home against newly-promoted Coventry. The likes of Declan Rice, Bukayo Saka and Martin Zubimendi are still yet to return after their World Cup exploits.

Dortmund, led by Niko Kovac, finished second in the Bundesliga last season, 16 points off winners Bayern Munich. They have played four pre-season friendlies thus far, winning twice and losing twice. The likes of Karim Adeyemi, Julian Brandt and Niklas Sule have left the club this summer.

#1532. When I overtook Jim Leighton, that was when I started to wind Kenny up about beating his cap tally... ANDY ROBERTSON on going level with Dalglish

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 17:28 EST, 12 November 2026 | Updated: 18:04 EST, 12 November 2026

It's a story which extols the virtues of loyalty and leadership in the proper sense.

More than anything, though, Andy Robertson’s achievements in football are – and always will be – reminders of what’s possible when a talented individual takes rejection as their motivation to redefine themselves in the eyes of the world.

Even though it’s been told many times before, the tale of the full-back’s determination to bounce back from being shown the door as a teenager by Celtic will never grow old.

Without having the character to overcome such adversity, he would not have been caught in the safety net at Queen’s Park. There would have been no moves to Dundee United and Hull. No Champions League and title-winning medals from his time with Liverpool. No first cap for his country.

In terms of a life lesson for those aspiring footballers who may find themselves in a cul-de-sac in their own careers, it has few equals.

All being well, Robertson will make his 102nd appearance for Scotland against North Macedonia, equalling the record tally of his idol and great friend, Sir Kenny Dalglish.

Andy Robertson will go level with Kenny Dalglish as Scotland's record cap holder on Friday

Both men are proud Glaswegians and Scots who bonded throughout their time together at Anfield. Dalglish would be the first to admit, though, that their respective paths have been distinct.

With a God-given talent so bright it could blind you, Dalglish was a superstar in the making before he wore a Scotland jersey for the first time against Belgium in 1971.

Coming in a friendly in Poland in 2014, Robertson’s first appearance only arrived after those early struggles.

It took huge character for him to even get that far. To add a century more across a dozen years under four different managers is a gargantuan achievement.

Football has a funny habit of throwing up strange co-incidences. Yesterday happened to be 40 years to the day since Dalglish won the last of his caps in a 3-0 win over Luxembourg.

Characteristically, before he took his own walk down memory lane, the man who’ll join him on that mark this evening was at pains to give the Anfield icon his rightful place.

‘It’s not really about me,’ Robertson insisted. ‘For how long the record stood, for starters, for what he (Dalglish) achieved in his career, for the person he is... tomorrow is another reason for our country to honour one of the greatest players that has played a game. He’s definitely the greatest in Scotland.

Dalglish scored 30 goals in his 102 caps and is regarded as Scotland's greatest ever player

‘Obviously, in terms of the number, I will stand side by side with him. But I don’t want people to forget how important this man has been to our country.

‘Because, for me, he was arguably the best player in the world at one time and will always be the greatest in this country, no matter what happens in the future.

‘He’ll always be the first one to do X, Y and Z. I just think that shouldn’t be forgotten.

‘Tomorrow is definitely a reason to do that for Kenny.’

There is, though, still no understating what Robertson has achieved across 12 years. Playing for Scotland wasn’t always the joy that it’s been in more recent times.

‘We get looked after so well off the pitch,’ he offered. ‘That probably wasn’t always the case when I first came in.

‘Under Gordon (Strachan) in my first qualifying campaign, I think I was still young enough to not think too much about it. But then I also remember under Alex McLeish and then the start of Steve Clarke, there was a real disconnect between the country and the players.

‘There wasn’t too much love for the players. We were getting 10,000, 15,000 inside Hampden. That was the most difficult time, especially as captain and being at Liverpool as well.’

He stuck at it and never shirked responsibility. In time he was able to chalk up the numbers because the side steadily improved and broke through the glass ceiling.

Robertson shares a laugh with Nathan Patterson ahead of the visit of North Macedonia

‘Of course, I would be sitting here with a few less caps if we hadn’t been successful,’ he reflected. ‘The fact that we got to two Euros, a World Cup and all the warm-up games and things like that resulted in me having an extra maybe 15 caps.

‘What makes it more special to me is the fact that we’ve managed to achieve things.’

All of this was beyond his wildest dreams at the beginning. A late substitute for Barry Bannan in a friendly in Warsaw on March 5, 2014, he can still hear Gordon Strachan whispering in his ear.

‘He basically said, “Don’t be scared, don’t go into your shell”,’ he recalled. ‘He said, “The reason I’ve picked you is because you’re brave. I see you bombing up and down the pitch for Dundee United”. He said, “Go and be that player”.

‘I always remember the first ball came to me and the words were ringing in my ears. I think I carried it 30 yards forward. It gave me the confidence to just go and try and play exactly the way I was playing under Jackie McNamara.’

Four years later, by then a Liverpool player, Robertson was handed the armband by McLeish following Scott Brown’s retirement.

‘That made me grow up and made me realise what it took to become a leader,’ he reflected. ‘I kind of grew into it. I believe that I became the captain that I wanted to be.’

It was only when he equalled McLeish’s 77 appearances that the prospect of one day equalling or surpassing Dalglish entered his head.

‘I think everyone in the room and everyone who personally knows me well enough knows that personal achievements aren’t really what I focus on,’ he said. ‘But I would lie if I said this wasn’t one that I’ve chased.

Like Dalglish, Robertson is a Liverpool icon having made 378 appearances for the Anfield club

‘I think when I overtook Darren Fletcher (80 caps), when I was in the 80s, it felt like ages for me to get to Jim Leighton (91). Then I thought I’ve only got one more person to go.

‘That’s when I started thinking about it a little bit more, starting to believe that it might happen, started to wind Kenny up a bit more that it was going to happen.

‘I think that was maybe when I realised that this was maybe possible if I got lucky with injuries, if I kept playing for Liverpool.

‘Sat here today, if it happens, it’s something I couldn’t be more proud of. My international career has been everything for me.’

To wear the armband at one international tournament would have been a laudable achievement in itself. To do so three times would have seemed an impossible feat in those difficult early days.

The hunger to repeat the trick at Euro 2028 is as strong as ever.

‘I’ve always kept pushing,’ he said. ‘We’re always trying something new. My wife asked me a similar question last week when we were talking about it. I was going to try and catch Gemma Fay (203 caps), but I think that might be a little bit too far from me...’

#1531. Everton dispatch Newcastle to give Matthias Jaissle a reality check

Everton appear well ahead of Newcastle United in their preparation for the new Premier League season after a comfortable 3-1 victory at Murrayfield.

On a sobering evening for new Newcastle manager Matthias Jaissle, who changed all 10 outfield players at half-time, Everton’s one and two-touch attacking play proved difficult to contain.

Everton took the lead through Thierno Barry after a defensive error from Sven Botman, before Iliman Ndiaye scored a penalty that was won cheaply by summer signing Hayden Hackney.

Newcastle’s raft of half-time changes helped David Moyes’s team strengthen their grip further, with Tyrique George adding a stylish third and 19-year-old Harrison Armstrong providing his second assist of the game.

Among the Newcastle players introduced at half-time was 18-year-old Sean Steur, the exciting midfield prospect signed from Ajax this summer. Aladji Bamba and Bazoumana Toure also flickered with promise, but a sharp start from Jaissle’s team faded.

They pulled a goal back late on when Jacob Murphy’s cross found Harvey Barnes at the back post, but they offered little as an attacking force throughout the second half.

Newcastle have two more friendlies, against Bayer Leverkusen and Strasbourg, before they begin their Premier League season at home to Liverpool.

The club are reeling from the summer departures of Bruno Guimaraes, Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and manager Eddie Howe, but David Hopkinson, the chief executive, struck a bullish tone when he spoke of this being the start of “Newcastle 2.0”.

Everton look the more settled side and club, and the performances of new arrivals Hackney and George were encouraging, while Thierno Barry was sharp in the centre-forward position that has proved so difficult for the club to fill in recent seasons.

Everton kick-off their new season at home to Crystal Palace, and keeping Ndiaye at the club beyond the end of the transfer window will be a priority.

The scoreline is a fair reflection of the game. Everton looked sharper, as well as fitter, and there are more positives for them to take. They look ready for the new season, Newcastle need reinforcements.

Alcaraz bends a shot not far wide from 25 yards for Everton. The game is meandering towards its conclusion now.

Willock collects the ball between the lines, feeds Murphy wide right, and his ball across goal is turned in at the back post by Harvey Barnes.

Moyes makes another pair of changes: Keane and Hackney off, O’Brien and Foster on.

Everton fans are enjoying themselves now, belting out Spirit of the Blues at Murrayfield.

More defending for Newcastle to do but they deal with Hackney’s corner delivery. All too easy for Everton to slice through their midfield in the build up though.

That goal had been coming, and Tyrique George is heavily involved again. He carries the ball forward and finds Armstrong, who returns the favour. George shoots on the swivel and picks out the bottom corner.

If I were a Newcastle fan in the stands, Edinbugh’s city centre hostelries would be looking very alluring just about now. There is not much for them to watch in this season half, they are chasing shadows. Some of that can be put down to the handful of young plyers in their second-half XI.

Tyler Dribbling drops a shoulder down the right, and wins a corner off Harvey Barnes. Everton are finishing this game the stronger, there are more goals in this should they put their foot on the pedal.

Newcastle, with some youngsters in their defence, looking a little ragged against Everton’s direct attacks now, but George runs into traffic at the edge of the box. Then Alcaraz is booked for a cynical foul.

Three more Everton changes on the way: Beto, Dibling and Alcaraz on for Barry, Ndiaye and Dewsbury-Hall.

Hayden Hackney plays a one-two with Tyrique George for Everton, with the former Chelsea winger backheeling the ball into Hackney’s path, and there were unheeded calls for a penalty. It was more of a penalty than the one Everton were awarded in the first half, Lewis Miley tripped him.

Thierno Barry’s performance has been a positive for Everton, could he nail down the No 9 role this season? It has been a problem position for several seasons now. Barry is tripped and Everton have a free-kick.

Dewsbury-Hall almost sneaks a shot in at the near post, but Hornicek tips the ball around the post.

Joe Willock with what was very nearly an exquisite disguised pass, but the flag was up for offside against Jacob Murphy.

Then an amusing moment: great cheers from the crowd as David Moyes heads a Hornicek clearance back down the line. He didn’t fancy the cushioned first touch off his instep, then.

Everton have played some quick one and two-touch football around the box in this game, and another move ends with George shooting over the bar. Everton are making their first change: Patterson off, replaced by Rohl.

The game is still finding its shape again after all those Newcastle changes, but Murphy did force a sharp save from Travers with a low shot from a tight angle.

He keeps to his word from before the game; Hornicek is the only player still on the pitch.

The players on for Newcastle are: Woltemade, Murphy, Willock, Barnes, Ramsey, Johnson, Steur, Pivas, Miley and Charlton.

It looks like an unchanged team from David Moyes, so Everton have a significantly more mature team on the pitch now.

Newcastle made a bright start, but as the half progressed there is no doubt that Everton have been the more dangerous attacking force and the scoreline reflects that. Here come the changes...

Everton have a late corner to defend, after another burst forward from Newcastle’s left-winger Toure. Newcastle try one off the training ground but the ball is cleared.

Thierno Barry almost finds the run of Hackney into the Newcastle penalty, and after a sluggish start, Everton have played some slick football in the attacking third.

A sign of some Newcastle frustration there was Wissa kicks Tyrique George across the shins. A bit naughty that, may even have been worthy of VAR attention in a Premier League game.

The Senegalese sends Hornicek the wrong way and finds the corner. No chance it was a penalty in the first place though, thankfully this is not a competitive game.

This is very soft, there was not much of a challenge by Joelinton on Dewsbury-Hall, but the Everton midfielder goes down in the box and is awarded the penalty.

It really should be 2-0 to Everton, a high-class moving down their left with Armstrong dinking a pass to Barry. He squared to Ndiaye who was free as a bird in the middle, but his shot was too close to Hornicek.

Joelinton runs down a blind alley before lumping a pass out for an Everton throw, and then the Newcastle man fouls Barry. The big Brazilian still finding his legs and getting up to speed.

A moment to forget for both Newcastle centre-backs. Thiaw was bumped and unbalance by Barry, before Botman steps out of defence and kicks fresh air against the Everton forward. Great recovery from Lewis Hall, but the ball breaks for Armstrong, who feeds Barry and he finishes across Hornicek.

Ndiaye has had a quiet start to the game for Everton, but his jinking qualities were on display there to beat a couple of Newcastle defenders. Everton lose the ball in midfield, and Tarkowski makes a superb last-ditch tackle to deny Osula.

Half-hearted appeals for a penalty from Wissa, but Hayden Hackney did not do much wrong. Looks like we will be spared a first-half hydration break, despite it being a sultry evening.

Osula skips through a couple of challenges at the edge of the area but fails to pick a pass in the box. Bazoumana Touré has looked lively for Newcastle on their left flank, and Bamba has done well for them in midfield.

Everton shake themselves into life as an attacking force. Cracking cross from Patterson into the box and Dewsbury-Hall’s run had gone untracked, but he was just stretching and could not generate enough power to beat Hornicek.

Good save from Travers to deny Elanga, but it was Mykolenko who made a hash of things in the box. The left back simply fell over the ball under no pressure. Newcastle the sharper of the two teams so far.

Joelinton feeds Bamba down the left wing for Newcastle who delivers a cross into the penalty area. Keane can only direct his defensive header back towards the penalty spot, but Wissa volleyed over with a first-time hit. Decent chance.

Thierno Barry makes it stick and proves a strong outlet for Everton. Botman brings him down at the expense of a free-kick just beyond the halfway line. Then Wissa drives into the penalty area for Newcastle after a one-two but he fouls Patterson.

Newcastle, playing in their lilac away kit, are the team trying to take the initiative with the ball, but Everton are quite happy staying compact and absorbing pressure. Elanga’s corner delivery is promising, but Osula does not connect cleanly at the back post.

Newcastle’s defenders enjoying comfortable possession in the early stages, Everton sitting off in their 4-4-2 defensive shape.

Wissa peels behind Everton’s defence inside the opening 90 seconds but he cannot lift the ball over Travers.

Bagpipes greet the players at Murrayfield, where the pitch has been reconfigured for football. There are only fans in the lower tier, and still plenty of empty seats even so.

We know it is a time in the pre-season when the legs are not that fresh, we train very intense but we want to play with an idea of how we want to play football. Intense with a vertical approach for sure, everyone gets 45 minutes except the goalkeeper.

Big Dunc and Moyes catch up pre-match! 🔵 pic.twitter.com/Jh4APHOZvX

A word that keeps being used about Jaissle is “special”. Newcastle’s hierarchy believe they have secured the services of a manager who will soon be recognised in the elite tier of European managers. We shall see how this view of the 38-year-old survives contact with a brutal and relentless Premier League campaign.

Newcastle XI: Hornicek; Shahar, Thiaw, Botman, Hall; Joelinton, Bamba; Elanga, Wissa, Toure; Osula

Newcastle subs: Gillespie, Harris, Charlton, Pivas, Johnson, M Miley, Finneran, Ramsey, Steur, Willock, J Murphy, Barnes, Neave, Woltemade

Your Mags at Murrayfield! ✊ pic.twitter.com/rDXpn0MqCg

Everton XI: Travers; Patterson, Tarkowski, Keane, Mykolenko; Hackney, Deswbury-Hall, Armstrong, Ndiaye; George, Barry

Here's how we start against Newcastle. UTT! 🔵📺 https://t.co/2VsWpyRq02 pic.twitter.com/vpnLPTRmLl

Newcastle United manager ​Matthias Jaissle is ‌refusing to dwell on the departure of key players that has left his club in turmoil going into the new season, as they step up their preparations against Everton at Murrayfield this evening.

Jaissle was recruited from Saudi Pro League side Al-Ahli after Eddie Howe left last month, with the German coach joining a club who have lost Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and captain Bruno Guimaraes in quick succession.

“It’s a challenge, a big challenge, always when there’s a transitional period. ‌But it’s ‌not time to ⁠complain, it doesn’t make sense to see the negative things,” Jaissle said.

“We want to see the chance in that situation and that’s our approach from day one. We are here to do our ⁠best job. We want to support the players, the current squad.

“There will be adjustments to see in the coming days, weeks. But for now it’s only focused on the daily work, the work we can influence. That’s all that ​matters now.”

The 38-year-old coach arrived in Newcastle ‌having won two Austrian Bundesliga titles with Red Bull Salzburg before leading Al-Ahli to back-to-back AFC Champions League crowns.

He remained tight-lipped about new signings.

“Obviously, in that transition phase, the players who left the club were ‌great ​players, great characters, experienced ⁠players. This is now a vacuum,” he said.

“Either we adjust something in the squad, by signing these players, these profiles, or other players ⁠need to step up and fill ​these positions, these leadership roles. I’m quite optimistic, we can work in both scenarios.”

Jaissle said he had a ​clear vision of how he wants his team to play.

“The phrase how Newcastle ‌should play like is front-footed, intense, ​aggressive and of course also successful. ​In the end, it’s all about what ⁠I can ⁠say and it’s also why I’m sitting here,” he said.

“The approach we have as a coaching team and the identity of Newcastle is famed for, it’s so linked so close together - which is a perfect fit in my eyes and ​that’s going to be exciting.”

#1530. A plant RNA-binding protein senses 2′,3′-cNMP produced by insect effectors

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

RNA-derived 2′,3′-cyclophosphate-terminated nucleotides act as immune signalling molecules in prokaryotes and eukaryotes1,2,3, but how plants perceive them remains unknown. Sucking insects inject digestive enzymes including RNases into the host plant to acquire nutrients. Here we demonstrate that NIB1, a glycine-rich RNA-binding protein in rice, senses 2′,3′-cyclic nucleotide monophosphates (2′,3′-cNMPs; 2′,3′-cAMP and 2′,3′-cGMP) and adenylyl-(3′→5′)-guanosine 2′,3′-cyclic phosphate (ApG>p) produced by a salivary T2 ribonuclease of green stink bug during feeding. Binding of the RNase products promotes formation of nuclear condensates containing NIB1, which recruit the core immune regulator Enhanced Disease Susceptibility 1 (EDS1) and activate defence, potentially contributing to the immune signalling of Toll/interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) proteins that also produce the nuclease products. Exogenous application of 2′,3′-cAMP, 2′,3′-cGMP or ApG>p elicits NIB1 and EDS1-mediated immune responses. Our findings unveil a conserved pathway in plants, in which glycine-rich RNA-binding proteins perceive the nuclease-generated second messengers to launch defence and point to a potential link between plant TIR nuclease activity and EDS1 signalling.

Insect pests cause losses to crop production and damage vegetation4,5. During feeding, insects release oral secretions containing proteins and other molecules that can activate or suppress host plant defence6,7,8. Digestive enzymes hydrolyse cellular components to generate nutrients for herbivores. These breakdown products also act as host-derived damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) that activate plant pattern-recognition receptors9,10. Identifying host-derived signalling molecules and their defence activation mechanisms is essential for developing new plant-protection strategies.

T2-family ribonuclease (RNaseT2) proteins, which preferentially cleave single-strand RNAs between purine and uridine residues, are ancient enzymes that are widely distributed across organisms and functional in diverse biological processes2,11. Plant S-RNases, which mediate self-incompatibility, belong to this protein family12. Phytopathogens also secrete nucleases into host tissues13,14. Human lysosomal RNaseT2 generates purine-2′,3′-cyclophosphate-terminated oligoribonucleotides that are sensed by Toll-like receptor 8 to activate innate immunity2. Toll/interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) domains of plant intracellular nucleotide-binding and leucine-rich repeat (NLR) immune receptors possess enzymatic activities towards oxidized nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) and nucleic acids15,16,17,18,19. Plant TIR domains generate second messengers such as 2′-ADPR and pRib-AMP, which promote the formation of EDS1–Phytoalexin Deficient 4 (PAD4)–Activated Disease Resistance 1 (ADR1) complex and trigger disease resistance15,20,21. Activated plant TIR also catalyses the production of ADPr-ATP and di-ADPR, leading to the complex formation of EDS1-Senescence-Associated Gene 101 (SAG101)–N Required Gene 1 (NRG1), inducing plant cell death16,22,23. Plant TIR domains also synthesize 2′,3′-cAMP and 2′,3′-cGMP (2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP) through nuclease activity. Arabidopsis nudix hydrolase 7 (AtNUDT7) hydrolyses 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and attenuates TIR-mediated cell death when overexpressed in Nicotiana benthamiana3. However, the contribution of 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP to EDS1-dependent immunity remains elusive.

Plant glycine-rich RNA-binding proteins (GRPs) encompassing one RNA recognition motif (RRM) at the N terminus and a glycine-rich region (GRR) at the C terminus regulate plant responses to abiotic and biotic stresses24,25. Arabidopsis GRP7 (AtGRP7) has a positive role in immunity, whereas the Pseudomonas syringae effector HopU1 suppresses AtGRP7-mediaed immunity by catalysing ADP-ribosylation of an arginine residue (R49) in the RRM of AtGRP726,27,28. These data indicate that the RRM of GRPs is central to immune function, although the underlying molecular mechanism remains unidentified. Here we report that the rice GRP NIB1 interacts with invading insect T2 RNases (such as NVR1) to promote ribonuclease activity and the production of 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p. Binding to the cyclic nucleotides via RMM stimulates NIB1 phase separation to assemble the plant defence machinery in the nucleus.

Nezara viridula (the green stink bug) is a polyphagous hemipteran pest feeding on a wide range of plants, including economically important food, fruit and vegetable crops and Nicotiana species. Populations of N. viridula have recently increased in rice fields. As a piercing-sucking mesophyll feeder (Fig. 1a), N. viridula uses needle-like stylets to puncture developing seeds or young leaves, extract nutrients and inject effectors29. To identify the secretory enzymes, we profiled proteins in its oral secretions using liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) and identified 22 putative digestive enzymes, of which 15 were likely to be secretory based on signal peptide prediction (SignalP 3.0 server) and de-redundancy (Blastp) (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Transient expression of these proteins in N. benthamiana leaves identified one candidate enzyme that induced severe cell death and reactive oxygen species (ROS) production within 3 days post-agroinfiltration (dpi) (Extended Data Fig. 1b,c). This protein shows high sequence similarity to ribonuclease and we named it N. viridula ribonuclease 1 (NVR1).

a, Fifth-instar nymph of N. viridula on rice panicle (left) and the adult on kidney beans (right). b, Diagram of NVR1 showing the N-terminal signal peptide (amino acids 1 to 24) predicted by Signalp 3.0 and the nuclease catalytic region (amino acids 28 to 235) predicted by Pfam. H indicates catalytically active histidine residues. c, Logo of conserved catalytically active sites (H64 and H116) in eukaryotic T2 RNases. d, Urea-PAGE separation of RNA digested by NVR1, NVR1(H116A), NVR1(H64A) and NVR1(H-doub). For gel source data, see Supplementary Fig. 1. e, Molecular structures of 2′,3′-cAMP, 2′,3′-cGMP and ApG>p. f, Extracted ion chromatogram comparison of NVR1 products with standards. The dinucleotide-2′,3′-cyclophosphate was produced from (UAGU)5 but was undetectable with (UGAU)5. rRNA, ribosomal RNA. g, Quantification of 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>P in rice leaves after 2 h of feeding by C. medinalis (Cm) third-instar larvae. ND, not determined. i, Quantification of 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p in N. benthamiana leaves 2 days post-expression of indicated protein (empty vector normalized to 1.0). j, Cell death in N. benthamiana leaves (3 dpi) induced by empty vector or wild-type or mutant NVR1. Colour-coded stacked bars display the percentages of each cell death score (0–5, n = 11 leaves). k, Hydrolysis of 100 μM 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p by 1 μM active and boiled AtNUDT7 at 25 °C for 16 h. l, AtNUDT7 (322 amino acids) suppressed the NVR1-induced cell death in N. benthamiana leaves after co-expression for three days (scored as in j). m,n, Quantitative PCR with reverse transcription (RT–qPCR) of MYC2 and NPR1 in NVR1-OE (m) and NVR1H-doub-OE (n) lines compared with wild type (ZH11). Data in d,f are representative of three independent experiments. Data in g–i,k,m,n are mean ± s.d. of n = 3 biologically independent replicates (h,k) or samples (g,i,m,n). Statistical differences were determined by two-tailed t-test (g) or one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s test (h,i,k,m,n).

NVR1 was predicted to have an N-terminal secretory signal peptide and no transmembrane region. Analysis using the protein family database (Pfam) revealed a ribonuclease (RNase) domain (Fig. 1b) that belongs to the RNaseT2 family11. NVR1 was detected both in N. viridula salivary glands and in infested rice plants, suggesting that it is secreted into plant tissues during feeding (Extended Data Fig. 1d). NVR1 exhibited a nucleocytoplasmic distribution pattern (Extended Data Fig. 1e).

H64 and H116 are conserved among T2 RNases from mammals, herbivorous insects, phytopathogenic fungi and plants (Fig. 1c and Extended Data Fig. 1f). NVR1 cleaved Cy5-labelled Arabidopsis tRNASer (83 nt) in vitro, whereas NVR1(H116A) and NVR1(H64A) mutants showed mild and strong reductions in substrate degradation, respectively, and the double mutant NVR1(H-doub) was almost completely inactivated (Fig. 1d), supporting H64 and H116 as key catalytic residues11. High-resolution mass spectrometry was subsequently used to identify products of the NVR1-catalysed reaction, which showed accumulation of 2′,3′-cAMP and 2′,3′-cGMP, as well as a dinucleotide-2′,3′-cyclophosphate with a mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) of 675.1072 in positive mode (Fig. 1e,f). Given that preferentially cleavage of single-stranded RNA between purines and uridines by RNaseT2 produces guanosine or adenosine 2′,3′-cyclophosphate termini2, we designed two oligoribonucleotides, (UAGU)5 and (UGAU)5, as substrates to determine the structure of the product. NVR1 exhibited activity towards (UAGU)5—but not towards (UGAU)5—generating a peak at 5.1 min in the extracted ion chromatogram mode that was identical to the dinucleotide-2′,3′-cyclophosphate peak at m/z 675.1072, suggesting that NVR1 produced 2′,3′-cGMP-terminated AMP (ApG>p). The ApG>p synthetic standard, eluting at 5.1 min with a m/z of 675.1072 in positive mode, aligns with the NVR1 product (Fig. 1f) and matches the tandem mass (MS2) spectrum (Extended Data Fig. 1g). The accumulation of 2′,3′- cAMP/cGMP and ApG>P was rapidly induced in rice leaves within 2 h after insect feeding (Fig. 1g).

The 2′,3′-cNMP and ApG>p synthase activity of NVR1 was dependent on the two catalytic histidines H64 and H116 (Fig. 1h). High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC)–mass spectrometry and matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization (MALDI) analysis showed that N. benthamiana leaves expressing empty vector or catalytic inactive NVR1 mutants accumulated much less 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p than leaves expressing wild-type NVR1 (Fig. 1i and Extended Data Fig. 1h). Leaves expressing NVR1 mutants were impaired in inducing plant cell death (Fig. 1j and Extended Data Fig. 1i). AtNUDT7 hydrolysed 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p (Fig. 1k). Co-expression with AtNUDT7 attenuated cell death activity of NVR1 in N. benthamiana at 3 dpi, with necrosis completed at 6 dpi (Fig. 1l and Extended Data Fig. 1j,k). These results indicate that the NVR1 enzymatic activity was causative to plant cell death.

To investigate plant responses to pest RNase, we generated rice NVR1-GFP transgenic plants that overexpress NVR1–GFP (Extended Data Fig. 2a,b). RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) analysis revealed that genes associated with biotic stimulus, jasmonic acid and defence were significantly enriched in NVR1-expressing plants (Extended Data Fig. 2c). MYC2, NPR1, COI1 and ERF1 (Fig. 1m and Extended Data Fig. 2d) were upregulated and levels of jasmonic acid and salicylic acid levels increased (Extended Data Fig. 2e). The Cnaphalocrocis medinalis ribonuclease 1 (CMR1), an NVR1 orthologue expressed by Cnaphalocrocis medinalis—a lepidopteran pest of rice—was detected in oral secretions and also produced 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP (Extended Data Fig. 2f,g), congruent with the rice leaf-feeding data (Fig. 1g). Given this functional conservation, we evaluated the resistance of NVR1 transgenic lines to C. medinalis. The larvae gained less weight on NVR1-expressing plants than on controls (Extended Data Fig. 2h). Adult females laid fewer eggs on NVR1 transgenic lines, and larvae preferred feeding on control plants (Extended Data Fig. 2i,j).

NVR1-expressing plants were stunted and produced fewer tillers, phenotypes associated with the growth cost of constitutive defence activation, whereas rice plants expressing catalytically inactive NVR1(H-doub) did not upregulate defence genes and grew normally (Fig. 1n and Extended Data Fig. 2k,l). These results demonstrate that heterologous expression of NVR1 in rice elicited defence responses and enhanced plant resistance to insect feeding, and that NVR1 catalytic activity is essential for immune activation.

To uncover the molecular mechanisms underpinning the NVR1-induced plant defence response, we screened plant proteins that could bind to NVR1 by immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry (IP–MS). NVR1-interacting RNA-binding protein 1 (NIB1 (Os03t0670700-04), also known as OsGRP330,31) showed a strong interaction signal (Extended Data Fig. 3a,b). NIB1 is a GRP composed of an N-terminal RRM and a C-terminal GRR and shares 80% N-terminal sequence identity with AtGRP726,27 (Extended Data Fig. 3c). Microscale thermophoresis (MST) indicated that NIB1 interacted directly with NVR1 in vitro (Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 3d), and co-immunoprecipitation confirmed the interaction in planta (Fig. 2b).

Statistical analyses used two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s post hoc test (f,h,j) or one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple-comparisons test (g,k). Split luciferase complementation (SLC) showed that the NIB1 RRM, but not the GRR, interacted with NVR1 (Extended Data Fig. 3e), matching the MST data (Fig. 2a). AlphaFold2 predicted the RRM residue R22 as a contact site (Extended Data Fig. 3f), and the NIB1(R22A) mutant abolished the interaction in planta (Extended Data Fig. 3g). NVR1 interacted strongly with NIB1, independently of its catalytic activity (Extended Data Fig. 3h–j).

Given that NVR1-like secretory T2 ribonucleases are widespread in insects and phytopathogenic fungi (Extended Data Fig. 1f), and GRPs are conserved across land plants (Extended Data Fig. 3k), we investigated whether the RNaseT2–GRP interaction is a common phenomenon. We tested secreted RNases T2 from the insect pests C. medinalis (CMR1) and Helicoverpa armigera (HAR1) and the fungal pathogen Magnaporthe oryzae (MOR1). SLC assays demonstrated that the recognition of T2-family RNases by plant GRPs is universal (Extended Data Fig. 3l,m).

Given that GRPs bind RNA fragments27 and NVR1 requires its RNase activity to elicit defence, we investigated the potential binding of NIB1 to the RNaseT2 products. NIB1–GST was incubated with NVR1 products, denatured to extract the bound molecules, and analysed by high-resolution mass spectrometry. Notably, high-intensity signals of 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p were observed (Fig. 2c). Structural modelling of NIB1 with ligands identified two adjoining residues in RRM domain loop, R49 and G50 that were responsible for 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP recognition (Fig. 2d and Extended Data Fig. 4a). R49 is a known RNA-binding site27, whereas G50 contacts both 2′,3′-cAMP and 2′,3′-cGMP in our model. G14 and W17 serve as additional recognition sites for ApG>p (Fig. 2d and Extended Data Fig. 4a). In MST assays with 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p, NHS-labelled NIB1 exhibited high binding affinity. Substitution of either residue with alanine (NIB1(R49A) or NIB1(G50A)) markedly reduced the binding affinity, and the NIB1(R49A/G50A/G14A/W17A) (hereafter NIB1(4A)) mutation fully abolished the ApG>p binding (Fig. 2e and Extended Data Fig. 3d). G14, W17, R49 and G50 are highly conserved in a group of GRPs across land plants (Extended Data Fig. 3n), implying a critical role of these residues in ligand recognition. The NIB1(R49A) mutation impaired NIB1 binding to both RNA and 2′,3-cyclic nucleotides, whereas the NIB1(G50A) mutant maintained binding affinity towards FLAGELLIN SENSITIVE2 (FLS2) 3′ untranslated region (UTR) while showing strongly impaired binding to 2′,3-cyclic nucleotides (Extended Data Fig. 4b). Thus, NIB1 employs shared yet distinct recognition mechanisms for 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and RNA.

In MST assays using 2′,3′-cAMP as a positive control, NIB1 did not bind 3′,5′-cAMP, 8-Br-3′,5′-cAMP, AMP or 2′,3′-cGAMP32 (Extended Data Fig. 4c–g). NIB1 exhibited 4-fold and 34-fold weaker binding affinities for 3′,5′-cGMP and GMP, respectively, compared with 2′,3′-cGMP (Fig. 2e and Extended Data Fig. 4h,i).

NIB1 contains a C-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR) (Extended Data Fig. 5a) that mediates phase separation33. PONDR predicted a high average disorder score similar to that of AtGRP7 (Extended Data Fig. 5b). In vitro, NIB1–YFP formed droplets that showed fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) and fused to form larger droplets (Extended Data Fig. 5c–e). NIB1–YFP signals also recovered after photobleaching in N. benthamiana leaves (Extended Data Fig. 5f).

To determine whether herbivory induces NIB1 condensation in planta, we generated two pNIB1::NIB1-YFP/ZH11 rice lines (Extended Data Fig. 5g). Following 6 h of feeding by third-instar C. medinalis larvae, distinct NIB1 nuclear condensates were clearly visualized (Fig. 2f), indicating that this phase separation is a physiologically relevant response to herbivory. Similar to the observations in vitro and in N. benthamiana nuclei, NIB1–YFP condensates in pNIB1::NIB1-YFP/ZH11 nuclei recovered fluorescence after photobleaching (Extended Data Fig. 5h).

We further analysed the interplay between NVR1 catalytic activity and NIB1 condensation. Wild-type NIB1–YFP, but not the C-terminal IDR-truncated NIB1(ΔIDR)–YFP, absorbed NVR1–mCherry into the droplets (Extended Data Fig. 5i–k). The droplets of purified NIB1–YFP protein with nucleic acid contamination, but not that of nucleic acid-free NIB1–YFP, were enlarged in the presence of NVR1–mCherry, whereas the catalytically inactive NVR1(H-doub)–mCherry did not exert such effect (Extended Data Fig. 5i–k). NIB1–YFP exhibited nucleoplasmic localization, and NVR1 significantly enhanced its nuclear accumulation, with about 70% of the examined nuclei containing distinct condensates. N-terminal YFP-tagged NIB1 showed a similar localization pattern (Extended Data Fig. 5l–n). Immunoblotting further confirmed that NVR1 promoted nuclear accumulation of NIB1 (Extended Data Fig. 5o). Nuclear condensates were not observed for the NIB1–NVR1(H-doub) or NIB1(ΔIDR)–NVR1 (Fig. 2g), revealing that the RNase activity of NVR1 is crucial for promoting NIB1 phase separation in the nucleus. In subsequent analyses, we focused on nuclear NIB1 condensates.

Multivalent interactions drive phase separation and locally concentrate molecules, as in dsDNA-dependent cGAS activation and NAD+/ATP-dependent plant TIR activation32,34. We investigated whether 2′,3′-cNMP and ApG>p would induce NIB1 phase separation. The NIB1(R49A)–YFP and NIB1(G50A)–YFP droplets were smaller than NIB1–YFP droplets with or without NVR1–mCherry (Extended Data Fig. 6a). When co-expressed with NVR1 in N. benthamiana, NIB1(R49A), NIB1(G50A) and NIB1(4A) did not generate sparkling nuclear condensates (Extended Data Fig. 6b), implying that NIB1 phase separation involves binding of 2′,3′-cNMP and ApG>p. Congruently, 2′,3′-cNMP and ApG>p (2 nM each) promoted NIB1 phase separation in vitro (Fig. 2h and Extended Data Fig. 6c,d), and treatment with 8-Br-2′,3′-cNMP or ApG>p increased nuclear condensates in N. benthamiana cells (Fig. 2i,j and Extended Data Fig. 6e). Notably, exogenous application of 50 µM 8-Br-2′,3′-cNMP and ApG>p for 6 h induced distinct nuclear condensates in the pNIB1::NIB1-YFP/ZH11 rice plant (Fig. 2k and Extended Data Fig. 6f), indicating that 2′,3′-cNMP and ApG>p act as agonists of NIB1 in promoting phase separation.

We further monitored NIB1–YFP condensation in N. benthamiana leaves upon treatment with nucleotide analogues. Consistent with findings from MST (Extended Data Fig. 4c–g), 3′,5′-cAMP, 8-Br-3′,5′-cAMP, AMP and 2′3′-cGAMP did not trigger condensate formation, whereas 3′,5′-cGMP and GMP induced far fewer condensates than 2′,3′-cAMP (Extended Data Fig. 6g,h). Co-incubation with NVR1, rice plant RNA (OsRNA) and 2′,3′-cAMP resulted in larger NIB1–YFP droplets in vitro, which required the NVR1 catalytic activity, NIB1 binding sites and 2′,3′-cAMP to achieve optimal effect (Extended Data Fig. 6i). In vitro reconstitutions revealed that NIB1–YFP formed droplets, dependent on 2′,3′-cAMP, OsRNA and salt, as well as protein and macromolecular crowding agent concentrations (Extended Data Fig. 6j–m).

To investigate the biochemical consequences of NIB1 liquid–liquid phase separation, we examined its effect on NVR1 enzymatic activity. NVR1 was more active in the presence of NIB1, and the substrate degradation increased with higher concentrations of NIB1 (Fig. 3a). When the C-terminal IDR-containing fragment was deleted (NIB1(ΔIDR)), the influence of NIB1 on NVR1 activity was reduced or negligible (Fig. 3b), suggesting that the IDR steers NIB1 to boost the NVR1 enzymatic activity. Consistently, the NVR1–NIB1 complex synthesized a higher amount of 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p than NVR1 alone, which also required the IDR in NIB1 for increased activity (Fig. 3c). Similarly, when co-expressed in N. benthamiana leaves, full-length NIB1 significantly enhanced NVR1 in generating 2′,3′-cNMP compared with NIB1(ΔIDR) (Extended Data Fig. 6n). We subsequently evaluated the effect of NIB1 on NVR1-induced cell death in N. benthamiana and found that removing the IDR from NIB1 largely abrogated its potentiation of NVR1-induced plant cell death (Extended Data Fig. 6o,p). Additionally, the NIB1(R49A) and NIB1(G50A) mutants also showed compromised acceleration of NVR1 catalysis (Fig. 3d) and the NVR1-induced plant cell death (Extended Data Fig. 6q,r). In sum, catalytically active NVR1 stimulates NIB1 phase separation, which in turn enhances NVR1 activity in degrading RNA and synthesizing 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p, thereby inducing plant cell death through a positive feedback loop. In this mutual potentiation interaction, NIB1 uses both the IDR and the RNA-binding sites in the RRM to amplify and transduce NVR1-generated signalling molecules.

Right, reaction completion after 25 min, calculated as (intensity of hydrolysed RNA)/(intensity of undigested RNA) × 100%. For gel source data, see Supplementary Fig. 1. b, Left, NIB1 (1 μM), but not NIB1(ΔIDR), stimulated NVR1 activity in a 25-min assay. Right, quantification of band intensity. For gel source data, see Supplementary Fig. 1. c, 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p produced by NVR1 (1 μM) after co-incubation with NIB1 or NIB1(ΔIDR) (1 μM) for 25 min. d, NIB1(R49A), NIB1(G50A) and NIB1(4A) (1 μM) activity in promoting the production of 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>p is compromised by NVR1 (1 μM), assayed for 25 min using rRNA as substrate (2 μg in 20 μl). In a–d, data are mean ± s.d. of n = 3 biologically independent replicates. Statistical differences were determined by one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple-comparisons test.

NIB1 is highly expressed in multiple rice tissues (Extended Data Fig. 7a). To investigate the NIB1 function in plant defence, we used CRISPR–Cas9 to generate NIB1-knockout (NIB1-KO) and NIB1-overexpression (NIB1-OE) rice lines (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 7b–d). NIB1-OE and NVR1-OE plants showed similar transcriptional changes, with 553 (59%) of the upregulated genes overlapping (Fig. 4b), including genes associated with response to biotic stimulus, jasmonic acid and defence (Fig. 4c). MYC2, NPR1, COI1 and ERF1 were downregulated in NIB1-KO plants but markedly upregulated in NIB1-OE plants (Extended Data Fig. 7e), consistent with the RNA-seq data and the levels of defence hormones salicylic acid and jasmonic acid (Fig. 4d). C. medinalis larvae gained more weight after feeding on the NIB1-KO lines than with the wild-type plants; by contrast, their growth was retarded on the NIB1-OE plants (Fig. 4e). Females and larvae preferred NIB1-KO over wild-type and NIB1-OE plants in oviposition and feeding-choice assays (Extended Data Fig. 7f,g). Insect feeding strongly induced MYC2 in wild-type rice, but the induction was much weaker in the NIB1-KO mutant (Fig. 4f). NIB1-OE plants had reduced tillering, partly resembling the NVR1-OE phenotype (Extended Data Fig. 2l), whereas NIB1-KO plants grew well and produced more tillers (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 7h), probably reflecting their differences in immune intensity. These results suggest that NIB1 positively regulates plant defence responses.

Right, colour-coded stacked bars display the percentages of each cell death score (0–5; n = 11 leaves). i, Jasmonic acid and salicylic acid contents in ZH11, NIB1-KO and NIB1-KO leaves expressing NIB1, NIB1R49A or NIB1G50A in 12-day old rice plants. j, 2′,3′-cNMP binding mutations impaired NIB1-mediated resistance to insect feeding. We next investigated whether the NVR1-induced plant defence responses were contingent on the presence of NIB1. Treatment of rice plants with purified NVR1 induced ROS production, which was attenuated in NIB1-KO lines (Fig. 4g). Consistently, NVR1-induced cell death was mitigated in NbGRP7-KO leaves compared with wild-type N. benthamiana (Fig. 4h and Extended Data Fig. 7i,j). Thus, the RNA-binding protein NIB1 mediates NVR1-dependent induction of plant defence response.

To further determine whether NIB1 senses 2′,3′-cNMP and ApG>p to mediate NVR1-induced immune activation, we generated overexpression complementation lines in NIB1-KO rice plants, including wild-type NIB1, NIB1R49A and NIB1G50A. The two recognition-deficient complementation lines were unable to rescue the immune responses in NIB1-KO mutants, as indicated by defence hormone accumulation (Fig. 4i), insect resistance (Fig. 4j and Extended Data Fig. 8a,b) and the expression of MYC2, COI1 and NPR1 (Extended Data Fig. 8c). Expression of NIB1R49A and NIB1G50A in wild-type rice plants did not lead to a clear upregulation of these defence genes (Extended Data Fig. 8d,e). Together, these results show that NIB1 activates plant defence against insect feeding and that sensing of 2′,3′-cNMP and ApG>p is crucial for this immune function of NIB1.

MST assays with NIB1(ΔIDR) exhibited similar binding affinity to 2′,3′-cAMP/cGMP and ApG>P as wild-type NIB1 (Fig. 2e and Extended Data Fig. 8f). However, overexpression of NIB1(ΔIDR)–YFP in NIB1-KO rice plants did not rescue the compromised insect resistance (Fig. 4k). Moreover, treatment with 50 µM 8-Br-2′,3′-cAMP induced condensate formation in pNIB1::NIB1-YFP/NIB1-KO plants but not in 35S::NIB1ΔIDR-YFP/NIB1-KO plants (Extended Data Fig. 8g,h). Thus, both ligand recognition via RRM and subsequent phase separation via IDR are essential for the NIB1-dependent defence response.

To connect the NVR1–NIB1 module to the plant defence network, we performed IP–MS on leaves co-expressing NIB1–YFP and NVR1. EDS1, CDPK and MAPK6 were identified as NIB1 interactors (Extended Data Fig. 9a). Comparison with the NVR1 interactome revealed that the shared components were enriched in herbivore-response pathways (Extended Data Fig. 9b).

EDS1 is a central immune signalling node35,36,37. In SLC assays, NIB1 interacted with rice EDS1 (Extended Data Fig. 9c). EDS1–YFP co-immunoprecipitated with NIB1–Flag in N. benthamiana (Fig. 5a), and His–NIB1 pulled down EDS1–Flag from N. benthamiana leaves (Extended Data Fig. 9d). Bimolecular fluorescence complementation (BiFC) assays showed that NIB1 interacted with EDS1 in the nucleus (Extended Data Fig. 9e), and the NIB1–EDS1 interaction was enhanced by NVR1 via its RNase activity (Fig. 5b). Catalytically active NVR1, but not the inactive NVR1(H-doub) mutant, stimulated NIB1 recruitment of EDS1 into sparkly nuclear condensates (Fig. 5c and Extended Data Fig. 9f). We then used EDS1–NES–mCherry to test whether EDS1 acts as a nuclear carrier for NIB1. When EDS1–NES–mCherry was largely retained in the cytosol, NIB1 continued to form nuclear condensates in the presence of NVR1 (Extended Data Fig. 9g), indicating that NIB1 nuclear condensation is independent of EDS1 and supporting the role of NIB1 as a scaffold for EDS1 recruitment.
